Chapter 2: Where corporate tax law lives

On 18 March 2026, the Finance Act 2026 received Royal Assent. Sixteen years earlier to the day, on 18 March 2010, the Taxation (International and Other Provisions) Act 2010 had received its own. TIOPA 2010 was the last product of a fourteen-year project to rewrite the UK’s direct tax statutes in a clearer, better ordered form. Its aim was to restate the law, not to change it.

FA 2026 went a step further than any rewrite Act. In its transfer pricing and permanent establishment rules, it points to texts written by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), and it tells us to read them as they stand from time to time, not as they stood on the day Parliament voted.

So where does corporate tax law actually live? In Acts and regulations, certainly. But also in treaties, in accounting standards that Parliament never wrote, in judgments, and now in international texts that change without a vote at Westminster. Around all of that sits a large body of HMRC guidance that is not law at all, yet shapes every enquiry.

This is the second chapter of Part One, and it is the book’s “how we know” chapter. The Living Law (TKS), chapter 2, explained statute, interpretation, the tribunals and the status of guidance. Here we go further, into the sources a larger company’s tax function uses every week. No single row of the syllabus grid is owned by this chapter, but the 2026 grid makes “Double tax treaties – application of OECD model and supplied extracts from treaties” and “Impact of accounting standards on taxable profits” core (grade 1), and Note 2 of the grid expects knowledge of the Law, Professional Responsibilities and Ethics, and Principles of Accounting manuals. We finish in the exam room, with what the screen gives you and what it does not.

The statute book a group lives in

Start with the Acts. As The Living Law, chapter 2, explained, statute is the law; everything else either interprets it or applies it. For a larger company the statute book is a handful of big Acts, and most of them come from the Tax Law Rewrite Project. The project began with a blueprint paper, Tax Law Rewrite: The Way Forward, in July 1996, and produced seven Acts: CAA 2001, ITEPA 2003, ITTOIA 2005, ITA 2007, CTA 2009, CTA 2010 and TIOPA 2010. The explanatory notes say the rewritten Acts do not generally change the meaning of the law. They restate it, in a new order.

The corporate statute map (FY2026)

Statute Spoken name (audio) What a larger company finds there
Corporation Tax Act 2009 (CTA 2009) “the two thousand and nine Act” The charge (s 2), its territorial scope (s 5) and residence (s 14); UK PE profits (ss 19–21, as rewritten by FA 2026); the foreign branch exemption (Part 2 Ch 3A, ss 18A–18S); trading income (Part 3, including s 46); loan relationships (Part 5); derivative contracts (Part 7); intangible fixed assets (Part 8); R&D (Part 13)
Corporation Tax Act 2010 (CTA 2010) “the twenty ten Act” Losses (Part 4); group and consortium relief (Part 5); carried-forward losses and the restriction (Parts 5A, 7ZA); change in ownership (Part 14); Part 22; distributions (Part 23); definitions (Part 24), including control (s 1124), the PE definition (ss 1140A–1144) and GAAP (s 1127)
Taxation (International and Other Provisions) Act 2010 (TIOPA 2010) “the International Act” Treaties and DTR (Part 2; Orders in Council under s 2); transfer pricing (Part 4); UTPP (new Part 4A, ss 217A–217T, FA 2026); APAs (Part 5); hybrids (Part 6A); CFCs (Part 9A); CIR (Part 10, Sch 7A)
Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992 (TCGA 1992) “the Gains Act” Company gains, groups (ss 171–181), share reorganisations, Sch 7AC SSE
Capital Allowances Act 2001 (CAA 2001) “the Capital Allowances Act” Plant and machinery, SBA, fixtures
Taxes Management Act 1970 (TMA 1970) “the Management Act” Appeals, group payment arrangements (s 59F), migration notices (s 109B), Sch 3ZB payment plans
FA 1998 Sch 18 “the company return rules in Schedule eighteen to the Finance Act nineteen ninety eight” CT returns, enquiries, determinations, discovery, return penalties
F(No.2)A 2023 Parts 3 and 4 “the Pillar Two legislation” Multinational and domestic top-up tax
Free-standing Finance Act schedules by name SAO (FA 2009 Sch 46); tax strategy (FA 2016 Sch 19); UTT (FA 2022 Sch 17)

Each year’s Finance Act mostly amends these Acts, so the amended Acts are what you read. But some rules never move into the main Acts: the senior accounting officer, tax strategy and uncertain tax treatment rules still live in schedules to the Finance Acts that introduced them. A researcher who searches only the Corporation Tax Acts will never find them.

Statutory instruments. Beneath the Acts sit regulations made by ministers under powers the Acts give them. They carry the same force of law and often hold the detail that costs money. Five run through this book:

SI Short name Why it matters
SI 1998/3175 Corporation Tax (Instalment Payments) Regulations 1998 the instalment payment regulations When large and very large companies pay (chapter 3)
SI 2004/3256 (the Disregard Regulations) the Disregard Regulations Keep certain exchange and hedging movements out of taxable profit for the time being (chapter 12)
SI 2004/3271 (change of accounting practice regulations) the COAP regulations Loan relationship and derivative transitions when a company changes its accounting framework (chapters 5, 12)
SI 2016/237 (country-by-country reporting) the CbC regulations €750m consolidated revenue threshold (reg 3) (chapters 1, 27)
SI 2023/818 Transfer Pricing Records Regulations 2023 the TP records regulations Master File and Local File for CT accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2023; UK-to-UK transactions excluded from the Local File (reg 6) (chapter 27)

Treaties arrive by yet another route. TIOPA 2010 s 2 provides that arrangements specified in an Order in Council, declared to have been made with a view to affording relief from double taxation, have effect (in accordance with s 6); s 5(2) requires a draft of the Order to be approved by resolution of the House of Commons first. So a treaty is negotiated by governments, but it reaches a company’s tax return only because Parliament has said it may.

When Parliament points at Paris

For most of the history of transfer pricing in this country, the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines entered UK law through a narrow, fixed door. TIOPA 2010 s 164 told the reader to construe Part 4 consistently with “the transfer pricing guidelines”. But the phrase meant one particular version, frozen in time, and a newer version counted only when the Treasury designated it by order. The July 2017 Guidelines were designated by SI 2018/266 for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2018; the 2022 Guidelines by SI 2022/1147 for corporation tax accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2023 (both as summarised in the sources listed in the notes).

FA 2026 opened the door wide. For chargeable periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026, UK law refers to the OECD’s materials in three places, and in the two most important it refers to them as amended or replaced from time to time:

Rule Provision (FA 2026) OECD material referred to Dynamic?
Transfer pricing TIOPA 2010 s 164(3)–(4C), substituted by FA 2026 Sch 6 para 18 Article 9 of the OECD Model Tax Convention approved by the OECD Council on 18 November 2025; the Transfer Pricing Guidelines 2022 (published 20 January 2022) Yes: as amended or replaced from time to time, subject to UK reservations; Treasury may opt out of an update by regulations
Attribution of profits to a UK PE CTA 2009 s 20(1A)–(1E), substituted by FA 2026 Sch 7 para 4 Article 7(2) of the 18 November 2025 Model and its Commentary; the 2010 Report on the Attribution of Profits to Permanent Establishments (22 July 2010); the TPG 2022; the March 2018 Additional Guidance Yes: as amended from time to time, subject to UK reservations; Treasury regulation power
The PE definition CTA 2010 s 1140A (new purpose clause), FA 2026 Sch 7 para 11 Article 5 of the 18 November 2025 Model and its Commentary Version named; whether the reference is dynamic was not confirmed (see notes)

HMRC’s International Manual describes the transfer pricing result plainly: the Model and the Guidelines are now interpretative aids whether or not a treaty is in place, and the references are to their most recent versions, with a Treasury power to opt out of specified updates (INTM414120).

Think of the statute as the rulebook and the OECD materials as the official commentary that the rulebook now tells the referee to read. The referee still applies the rulebook. But when a rule could bear two meanings, the referee must prefer the one that fits the commentary, and the commentary is updated in Paris.

Why would Parliament do this? Because transfer pricing and PE disputes are fought between tax authorities, under treaties, through mutual agreement procedures. A UK rule that drifted from the international reading would invite double taxation. The cost is a loss of control: Parliament no longer votes on each change of reading, so the Treasury’s power to switch off an update is the safeguard. Chapter 23 owns the “authorised OECD approach” to PE attribution; chapter 27 owns transfer pricing.

The misconception: “the OECD Guidelines are just guidance”

The misconception runs like this. The OECD cannot legislate for the UK; its documents call themselves guidelines and commentaries; so they are just guidance, like HMRC’s manuals, to be quoted when helpful and ignored when not.

People believe it for good reasons. The OECD is not a parliament. Its Model is a template that each pair of countries adapts. And for most of the corporation tax code it remains true that nothing outside the statute and the cases binds you.

For transfer pricing it has not been true for a long time, because s 164 has long required consistency with the designated Guidelines. What FA 2026 adds is reach and currency: the PE rules now carry the same kind of instruction, and the transfer pricing reference follows the texts as they change. Ignoring them is not choosing a different view of the guidance; it is misreading the statute. An argument about the arm’s length price of an intra-group loan, or about how much capital a branch should be treated as having, must now be built from two things together: the words of the Act and the OECD text the Act points to.

Two limits keep the picture honest. First, the OECD texts guide interpretation. They do not override clear statutory words, and the UK’s reservations and any Treasury opt-out still apply. Second, the texts are long and they change. This book could not open the OECD’s own website (oecd.org refused access during the research), so where it describes the Guidelines it relies on the statute and on HMRC’s descriptions, and says so.

There is also an exam wrinkle. The examination screen gives you the OECD Model as a PDF of the 2017 articles, while FA 2026 points to the version approved in 2025. In the exam, use what you are given, and use a supplied treaty extract in preference to either.

Going further: building an argument from statute plus OECD text. A defensible technical position on a TP or PE point now has four layers, in this order: (1) the UK statute in force for the chargeable period (check commencement); (2) the OECD text the statute names, in the version it names, and any later version if the reference is dynamic, checking UK reservations and any Treasury opt-out regulations; (3) HMRC’s manual, as the reading the inspector will put forward (INTM414000 onwards for the reformed TP rules); (4) case law, remembering that pre-2026 judgments were decided on older wording. A memo that skips layer 2 on a TP point is now incomplete as a matter of statutory construction, not just of persuasion.

Exam lens: sources and the OECD materials. - Grade: DTTs, “application of OECD model and supplied extracts” 1 (core); transfer pricing and APAs 1 (core) (2026 grid; check the 2027 grid when published). Note 2: knowledge of the Law, PR&E and Principles of Accounting manuals’ terms is expected. - Past appearances: N23 Q1 (20 marks: residence with a supplied treaty tie-breaker extract; examiners: some “ignored the supplied treaty article and used the OECD Model text instead”); N23 Q6 (20 marks: TP methods from the OECD Guidelines; theory good, functional analysis weak). - Style: source-awareness is never asked for as such; it earns marks indirectly, by citing the right statute and applying the right version. - Traps: using the OECD Model PDF where an extract is supplied; quoting HMRC guidance as if it were law; applying FA 2026 rules to a period that began before 1 January 2026.

Treaties, and the judges who read them

A double tax treaty is an agreement between two states. In the main it allocates taxing rights and limits what each state may take; it is not a free-standing source of tax charges. Its words were negotiated by officials, usually following the OECD Model, and they are read differently from a UK statute. A treaty is meant to mean the same thing in both countries, so its words take an international meaning rather than a purely domestic one.

The leading modern authority is Fowler v HMRC [2020] UKSC 22, decided by the Supreme Court on 20 May 2020. Mr Fowler was a diver resident in South Africa who worked in the UK sector of the continental shelf in 2011/12 and 2012/13. UK domestic law (ITTOIA 2005 s 15) deems an employed seabed diver to be carrying on a trade. Mr Fowler argued that the deeming carried through into the UK–South Africa treaty, so that his income fell under the business profits article, which South Africa alone could tax. The Supreme Court unanimously disagreed. Lord Briggs, giving the judgment, held that the domestic deeming rule did not change which treaty article applied; treaty words take their ordinary international meaning, and the income fell under the employment article, so the UK could tax it.

On the OECD Commentaries, Lord Briggs said they carry persuasive force “as the cogency of their reasoning deserves”, even where a Commentary post-dates the treaty. That describes the general position for treaties. FA 2026 goes further for transfer pricing and PEs, because there the statute itself directs you to the OECD texts.

Treaties also change in bulk now. The Multilateral Instrument (MLI), in force for the UK from 1 October 2018, modifies many treaties at once, and HMRC publishes synthesised texts showing how each covered treaty reads after the modification. The UK–Ireland synthesised text is an example: it applies, among others, MLI Art 7, the principal purpose test, which denies a treaty benefit where “it is reasonable to conclude … that obtaining that benefit was one of the principal purposes of any arrangement or transaction”, unless granting it would accord with the object and purpose of the treaty. So a tax function reading a treaty asks three questions: which text applies after the MLI; what its words ordinarily mean in context; and whether a purpose test could take the benefit away. Chapter 24 owns treaties in depth.

The accounts as a source of tax numbers

The largest source of numbers in a corporation tax computation was not written by Parliament at all. It was written by accounting standard setters.

CTA 2009 s 46(1): the profits of a trade “must be calculated in accordance with generally accepted accounting practice, subject to any adjustment required or authorised by law”. The loan relationship and derivative rules go further: the amounts brought into account are, in general, those recognised in determining profit or loss under GAAP (CTA 2009 ss 307–308; ss 595, 597). CTA 2010 s 1127 defines GAAP to cover both UK GAAP and international accounting standards. In practice that means the Financial Reporting Council’s standards, chiefly FRS 102 and the reduced disclosure framework in FRS 101, or full IFRS for listed group accounts (HMRC BIM31020; CFM20030).

Why build tax on accounts? Because they exist already, they are audited, and they follow a consistent logic from year to year. A second, tax-only set of books for every company in a group would be costly and easy to manipulate. So the law starts from the accounts and then adjusts them where policy demands: capital allowances replace depreciation; entertaining is disallowed.

The courts have generally held to this line. In HMRC v NCL Investments Ltd [2022] UKSC 9, HMRC argued that IFRS 2 debits for employee share options should be disallowed; it lost on every ground, and the debits followed the accounts. The line has limits. In GDF Suez Teesside Ltd v HMRC [2018] EWCA Civ 2075, the old FA 1996 requirement that amounts “fairly represent” the profits required a credit that GAAP-compliant accounts did not show.

The consequence is easy to miss: when a standard changes, taxable profit can change without any Finance Act. ICAEW commentary (23 March 2026) notes that the FRS 102 periodic review, effective for periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026, brings most leases onto the balance sheet and that the net transition amount generally falls into the first period on the new basis, which can push companies into instalments for the first time [secondary]. A tax function therefore reads accounting standard updates as closely as Finance Bills. Chapter 5 owns the detail (s 46, change of basis under ss 180–187, leases); chapter 6 owns the tax charge in the accounts.

Exam lens: accounts as a source. Grade: “Impact of accounting standards on taxable profits” 1 (core); the Prospectus expects “an understanding of current accounting issues relevant to tax such as deferred tax, profit recognition and share schemes”. Past appearances: tax-accounting tails in M24 Q2(b), M25 Q2(b), N25 Q1(b) and a 10-mark deferred tax question in M26 Q6. Trap: forgetting that a non-tax accounting change (a framework move or a revised standard) can create a taxable adjustment.

HMRC’s view, and asking first

HMRC publishes thousands of pages of manuals. For a larger company the main ones are:

Manual Code Typical use in this book
International Manual INTM Treaties (INTM153000 series), DTR (INTM164000 series), CFCs, branch exemption, transfer pricing (reformed guidance from INTM414000)
Corporate Finance Manual CFM Loan relationships, derivatives, CIR background (CFM95110–95130)
Company Taxation Manual CTM Returns, instalments (CTM92520), losses, change of ownership
Corporate Intangibles Research and Development Manual CIRD Intangibles, R&D, CIR guidance
Capital Gains Manual CG Company gains, groups, SSE
Business Income Manual BIM Trading profits, GAAP (BIM31020, BIM31095)
Business Leasing Manual BLM Leasing
Senior Accounting Officers Guidance SAOG SAO duties and penalties

Around them sit policy papers, consultation outcomes and tax information and impact notes (TIINs), which explain why a measure was introduced.

Their status is simple to state. A manual is HMRC’s view of the law. It is not law. A tribunal is not bound by it, and where it conflicts with the statute, the statute wins. Manuals also date: some INTM transfer pricing pages still carry a note that the rules were reformed by Finance Bill 2025-26 and point to draft guidance at INTM414000 for periods from 1 January 2026.

Yet for a larger company HMRC’s view has a sharper edge. Under the uncertain tax treatment rules (FA 2022 Sch 17), a qualifying company whose treatment relies on an interpretation not in accordance with HMRC’s known position (published guidance or dealings with HMRC), with a tax advantage over £5m, must notify HMRC (paras 10, 11, 18). Chapter 4 tells that story. So the manuals are not law, but departing from them can create a legal duty to say so.

The practical lesson: read the manual as the argument your inspector will make, test it against the statute and the cases, and record why you agree or disagree.

Asking first. Sometimes the best source of law is an answer from HMRC in advance. There are three main routes, plus APAs for transfer pricing.

Route Legal basis When What you get
Statutory clearance In the Act concerned: e.g. demergers CTA 2010 s 1091; share exchanges and reconstructions TCGA 1992 s 138; transactions in securities CTA 2010 Part 15 (30 days for HMRC to respond; 30 more after any request for information) Transactions where the law turns on purpose Binding on HMRC on the facts disclosed
Non-Statutory Clearance Service HMRC guidance Genuine uncertainty about how the law applies to a specific transaction Written confirmation of HMRC’s view; HMRC will not act as a “confirmation service”, advise on tax planning or clear arrangements designed to avoid tax; a statutory route takes precedence
Advance tax certainty for major projects FA 2026 ss 266–274 A qualifying investment project expected to involve at least £1bn of UK expenditure over its life Clearance binding on HMRC for up to 5 years, subject to unchanged facts and law; service opened 1 July 2026; published scope excludes transfer pricing, valuations, purpose tests and the GAAR [launch date and exclusions: secondary sources]
Advance pricing agreement TIOPA 2010 Part 5 (ss 218 onwards) Transfer pricing, PE attribution The Tax Acts apply in accordance with the agreement for covered periods (chapter 27)

Going further: when to ask. A clearance costs time, discloses your thinking and fixes the facts you must then follow. Not asking leaves the risk on the balance sheet and, for a large business, may trigger UTT if the position departs from HMRC’s known view. Good practice in a tax function: keep a clearance log; build the statutory clearance timetable into the deal timetable (a demerger or share exchange cannot sensibly complete before clearance); use the non-statutory route only where you can show genuine uncertainty; and use an APA where a recurring transfer pricing question carries real money (chapter 27, Tarnmoor’s bilateral APA in GY6).

Case law, and the echo of Europe

The tribunal ladder is as The Living Law, chapter 2, described it: First-tier Tribunal (Tax Chamber), Upper Tribunal (Tax and Chancery Chamber), Court of Appeal, Supreme Court. A First-tier decision binds no later tribunal, though it can persuade; the Upper Tribunal and the courts above it make precedent.

Since April 2022 the National Archives has published judgments free of charge through Find Case Law (caselaw.nationalarchives.gov.uk), searchable by neutral citation, party and judge. Most of the corporate cases in this book, from BlackRock HoldCo 5, LLC v HMRC [2024] EWCA Civ 330 in the prologue to the unallowable purpose cases in chapter 12, can be read there in full, and so can First-tier decisions such as DSG Retail Ltd v HMRC [2009] UKFTT 31 (TC). Read the judgment, not a summary. Two habits help: note the court (a Court of Appeal judgment outranks a First-tier decision however recent), and check what happened next (a pending appeal, such as Syngenta Holdings Ltd v HMRC, where the Upper Tribunal granted permission in [2025] UKUT 338 (TCC), can change the answer).

The echo of Europe. While the UK was a member state, the Court of Justice tested UK tax rules against freedom of establishment. In Cadbury Schweppes plc v IRC (Case C-196/04), judgment 12 September 2006, it held that CFC-type rules could be justified only against “wholly artificial arrangements”. Marks and Spencer, the cross-border group relief litigation that The Living Law, chapter 24, described, shaped the rules on foreign losses. The present CFC regime (TIOPA 2010 Part 9A, from 2012) was built partly in answer to that case law, and its finance company exemption then spent years in a State aid dispute: Commission decision 2 April 2019; annulled by the Court of Justice on 19 September 2024 [dates from secondary sources]; SI 2024/1307 and FA 2026 s 51 dealt with the repayments.

Brexit has not erased that history. Since the end of 2023 the principle of the supremacy of EU law is not part of UK domestic law, and what was “retained EU law” is now “assimilated law” (Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023). But the rules shaped by those judgments remain on the statute book, and the judgments still explain why they look as they do. Chapters 22, 25 and 26 return to them.

Reading the law on the right day

A section of TIOPA 2010 does not have one meaning. It has a meaning on a date, and the online text you read may not be the text that applies to your client’s period.

The free official source is legislation.gov.uk. Each page carries a “Changes to legislation” box stating the date up to which the text is up to date with changes known to be in force, and listing effects the editorial team has not yet applied (“outstanding” or “changes not yet applied”). When that box lists outstanding effects, the text on screen may be out of date. The site also keeps point-in-time versions: you can read CTA 2010 s 1141 as it stood on 31 December 2025 (old dependent agent test: an agent who “has and habitually exercises there authority to do business on behalf of the company”) beside the current version (a person who “habitually concludes contracts, or habitually plays the principal role leading to the conclusion of contracts…”). Pending effects are not shown on point-in-time views.

The site also holds each Act as enacted (add /enacted to the URL, e.g. FA 2026 is ukpga/2026/11). The revised text shows the law as amended; the enacted text shows what the amending Act did and from when. Commencement rules often sit at the end of a Schedule: for the UK-to-UK exemption, FA 2026 Sch 6 para 32(1).

Commencement in practice (real-calendar illustration, not the Tarnmoor story). Most of FA 2026’s international changes (PE definition and attribution, transfer pricing, UTPP) apply to chargeable periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026:

Company’s accounting period FA 2026 PE / TP / UTPP rules?
1 January 2026 – 31 December 2026 Yes, for the whole period
1 April 2025 – 31 March 2026 No: old rules (and DPT) for the whole period; new rules from the AP beginning 1 April 2026
1 October 2025 – 30 September 2026 No: old rules for the whole period, although most of it falls after 1 January 2026

So the same section, read on the same day, can give different answers to three companies. Ask three questions every time: which version applies to this period; has the site applied every change; and what does the Act as enacted say about commencement?

Going further: coming next. The draft Finance Bill 2026-27 (published 13 July 2026) includes reform of the foreign PE exemption, including a further amendment to CTA 2010 s 1140A for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027 in the draft legislation. This is proposed, not law, and not examinable on FA 2026.

Tom Hesketh’s question

Our invented group, Tarnmoor, the listed UK engineering group introduced in chapter 1. Every company and person in it is invented.

In the first weeks of GY1, Tarnmoor’s group head of tax, Tom Hesketh, receives a question from the CFO, Nadia Kerr.

The group’s treasury company, Tarnmoor Finance Ltd (TFL), has lent £430m to four UK group companies, all at 6%. It has also lent £120m to Tarnmoor Vallaria SA (TVS) in the invented country of Vallaria. And Tarnmoor plc has lent £20m, interest free, to Tarnmoor Ireland Ltd (TIL), which is incorporated in Ireland but, on our invented facts, centrally managed and controlled from Leeds and so UK resident.

Tarnmoor’s consolidated revenue (GY1 £1,180m, about €1,357m at the story’s assumed €1.15 per £) is far above €750m, so its UK companies already keep a Master File and Local File under SI 2023/818, which already leaves UK-to-UK transactions out of the Local File (reg 6). Nadia’s question goes further: does the pricing of the UK loans still have to be tested at all? Tom does not answer from memory, because the law on this point was rewritten by FA 2026. He sets his team a research memo, and it follows the order of this chapter.

Why the question arises. The transfer pricing rules (then ICTA 1988 Sch 28AA) originally applied only to transactions between a UK and an overseas person. FA 2004 (ss 30–37) extended transfer pricing and thin capitalisation to UK-to-UK transactions for chargeable periods beginning on or after 1 April 2004 (INTM413250). The change followed the Court of Justice’s judgment in Lankhorst-Hohorst (2002), which held that national thin capitalisation rules could in principle breach freedom of establishment; the usual explanation is that the UK chose to apply its rules at home too, an explanation, not something the statute says. Two decades later the Corporate Tax Roadmap (October 2024, para 2.48) said that “the potential removal of UK-to-UK transfer pricing … would reduce the UK compliance burden”. FA 2026 did it.

Testing the exemption

Worked example 2.1: the research memo on TIOPA 2010 s 164A (in our invented case, GY1)

Step 1: statute. TIOPA 2010 s 164A, inserted by FA 2026 Sch 6 para 16: s 147(3) and (5) do not apply to “qualifying UK to UK provision”. HMRC guidance: INTM414320 (the exemption) and INTM414330 (transfer pricing notices).

Step 2: commencement. Chargeable periods commencing on or after 1 January 2026 (FA 2026 Sch 6 para 32(1)). Every Tarnmoor story period runs on FA 2026 law, so the exemption is available from GY1.

Step 3: conditions (s 164A(2) and (5); INTM414320).

Condition Tarnmoor’s four UK loans Point to check
Both affected persons UK-resident companies, within the charge to CT on the relevant profits TFL, TEL, TPLC, TES, TWS: all UK-incorporated and UK resident —
Same rate of CT All profitable UK members pay 25% (with a marginal relief divisor of 9 in GY1 the upper limit is about £27,778 per company) TPLC has excess management expenses and no taxable profits most years: read the exact wording of the rate condition
Same reference currency Sterling throughout —
No one-sided s 589 derivative; no s 18A exemption adjustments; not patent box provision None —
Neither party an excluded company (e.g. banking company, ring fence, tonnage tax, BLAGAB life, OEICs, AUTs, investment trusts, UK REITs, securitisation companies, QAHCs, electricity generator levy and RPDT cases) TFL is a group treasury company taking no deposits Read the statutory definition of “banking company” rather than relying on the label

Step 4: off-switches. An irrevocable election that the exemption is not to apply (per provision or per period); and an HMRC transfer pricing notice where expedient to prevent a loss of tax judged across both parties, normally only after a notice of enquiry, appealable on the ground that there is no such loss.

Step 5: purpose (INTM414320). Where both parties are taxed in the UK at the same rate, compensating adjustments under s 174 usually make UK-to-UK pricing tax neutral; the exemption removes compliance cost while HMRC keeps a power to act where a net loss of tax could arise.

The loans (£m, a year)

Lender → borrower Principal Rate Interest Within s 164A?
TFL → TEL 200.0 6% 12.0 Yes
TFL → TPLC 120.0 6% 7.2 Yes (subject to the rate-condition check)
TFL → TES 70.0 6% 4.2 Yes
TFL → TWS 40.0 6% 2.4 Yes
UK-to-UK total 430.0 25.8
TFL → TVS (Vallaria) 120.0 6% 7.2 No: cross-border; full Part 4 (chapter 27)
TPLC → TIL 20.0 nil nil Yes while TIL is UK resident; full Part 4 if it ceases to be

TFL’s lending: £550m in total (matching its £550m 5.5% notes, interest £30.25m), of which £430m (78%) is UK-to-UK.

Illustration: why the old rule protected nothing (labelled hypothetical, not a story fact). Suppose an arm’s length rate for TEL’s loan had been 5.5% rather than 6%.

£
Excess interest: £200m × (6.0% − 5.5%) 1,000,000
TEL: deduction disallowed under s 147(3); extra CT at 25% 250,000
TFL: compensating adjustment claim (s 174), interest income reduced; CT saved at 25% (250,000)
Net effect on the group’s UK tax nil

Conclusion (in our invented case). No TP adjustment on the four UK loans; the Vallarian loan stays fully within Part 4; the TIL loan qualifies only while TIL remains UK resident. The exemption switches off one rule, not the code: unallowable purpose (CTA 2009 s 441, chapter 12) and the corporate interest restriction (chapter 28) still apply to every one of these loans. The memo feeds chapters 12 and 27.

Going further: the tax function’s tasks. (1) Record the s 164A analysis for each UK-to-UK provision and re-test it each period (a change of residence, a company becoming a bank or a QAHC, or a patent box election can take a provision out). (2) Decide whether any election out is wanted: advisers have noted that groups may sometimes prefer arm’s length pricing where other rules depend on it [secondary, RSM]. (3) Keep the cross-border pricing (TVS) and its Master File and Local File in order. (4) Remember that the CIR and Pillar Two computations, not transfer pricing, now carry most of the weight on intra-UK financing.

Exam lens: s 164A. Grade: within transfer pricing 1 (core). Past appearances: none yet (new in FA 2026; first examinable in 2027 sittings on FA 2026). Likely angle: a UK group with UK and overseas subsidiaries where candidates must say which intra-group loans need TP (cross-border, and UK-to-UK only if a condition fails) before computing a CIR. Traps: applying s 164A to a cross-border loan or to a CFC (s 371SD(5A)); forgetting that the SME exemption (s 166) is a different rule; assuming the exemption also switches off s 441 or CIR.

Research in the exam room

On the day of the exam, the sources shrink. The paper is closed book, sat on RM Assessment Master (replacing Exam4 from the October 2026 sitting). Behind the “open book” icon you will find: the tax tables (also on your desk in hard copy); the OECD Model Convention as a PDF of the 2017 articles, available only on screen; and links to Croner-i or Tolley student legislation, which you must buy in advance (work subscriptions will not log in).

You cannot make notes in either legislation product. You may highlight, and you may tag: a tag may carry a section number or a topic name (the CIOT’s example: “Corporate rescue exception = CTA 2009 (s 361D)”), but not a pro forma or formula, and invigilators may spot-check.

Navigation map to practise now

Regime Where Sections worth tagging
Transfer pricing TIOPA 2010 Part 4 s 147 (basic rule), s 148 (participation), s 155 (potential advantage), s 164 (OECD interpretation), s 164A (UK-to-UK), s 166 (SME), s 174 (compensating adjustments)
CFCs TIOPA 2010 Part 9A s 371BC (charge), Ch 3 (gateway), Chs 10–14 (exemptions)
CIR TIOPA 2010 Part 10; Sch 7A Part 10 contents page; s 392 (interest capacity); Sch 7A (reporting company)
Hybrids TIOPA 2010 Part 6A contents page
DTR TIOPA 2010 Part 2 s 2, s 18, s 42, s 52, s 58
PE CTA 2010 ss 1140A–1144; CTA 2009 ss 19–21 s 1141 (definition), s 1142 (independent agents), s 1143 (preparatory or auxiliary)

Practise with the product you will use on the day: each publisher lays out the Acts and its search differently.

The examiners have also told candidates how to use treaty material. After N23 they reported that some candidates ignored the supplied treaty article and used the OECD Model instead. When a question supplies an extract, the extract is the treaty for that question. Use the Model only when nothing else is given, and quote the article number so the marker can follow you.

The exam does not test your ability to find an obscure manual page, and it rewards statute over guidance. It does test whether you know which rule applies to which period, so state the law year you are applying. For a 2027 sitting that will almost certainly be FA 2026 (FY2026), and the 2027 tax tables, when the CIOT publishes them (not yet published at 9 October 2026), will show it.

Exam lens: research under exam conditions. - Resources: tax tables (paper and PDF), OECD Model (2017 articles, PDF only), Croner-i or Tolley online legislation; nothing else; no watches; two sheets of note paper (not marked). - The spreadsheet rule: “Calculations left in the spreadsheet and not copied to the answer box will not be marked” (Candidate Instructions, October 2026); examiners cannot see formulae. - Rubric: “All workings should be shown and made to the nearest month and pound unless the question specifies otherwise.” - Style: no letter, report or email format in LCG AT; technical prose and computations; 10, 15 or 20-mark questions; 0.5–1 mark per point. - Traps: citing a manual as authority; using the Model over a supplied extract; citing pre-FA 2026 PE sections (old ss 22–32 CTA 2009 are omitted for periods from 1 January 2026). Chapter 32 owns exam craft in full.

What to take away

Corporate tax law lives in several places at once, and a tax function needs to know which kind of source it is holding.

  • Statute first. CTA 2009 computes profits; CTA 2010 gives reliefs and structure; TIOPA 2010 holds DTR, TP, CFCs, hybrids and CIR; TCGA 1992, CAA 2001, TMA 1970 and FA 1998 Sch 18 complete the core, with free-standing schedules for SAO, tax strategy and UTT. SIs carry equal force; treaties take effect by Order in Council under TIOPA 2010 s 2.
  • OECD materials in statute (FY2026). TIOPA 2010 s 164 (TP), CTA 2009 s 20(1A)–(1E) (PE attribution) and CTA 2010 s 1140A (PE definition) refer to the Model and Commentary approved on 18 November 2025 and the TPG 2022; for TP and attribution, as amended from time to time; chargeable periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026. There the Guidelines are not “just guidance”. Elsewhere, Fowler: Commentaries persuade “as the cogency of their reasoning deserves”.
  • Accounts supply most of the numbers (CTA 2009 s 46; ss 307–308), so a change of accounting standard can change taxable profit without a Finance Act.
  • HMRC’s manuals are its view, not law; but departing from its known position can trigger a UTT notification above £5m.
  • Certainty in advance: statutory clearance where one exists; the non-statutory service only for genuine uncertainty; the advance tax certainty service for projects of at least £1bn (binding up to 5 years); an APA for TP.
  • Read the law on the right day: “Changes to legislation” box; point-in-time versions; commencement words applied precisely.
  • In our invented case, Tarnmoor’s four UK loans (£430m at 6%) fall within the UK-to-UK exemption in s 164A; the Vallarian loan stays inside transfer pricing.

The next chapter turns from where the law lives to how a large group lives with it: returns, payments and enquiries.

Chapter three: Returns, payments and enquiries

Part One: The Larger Company

When should a company pay tax on profits it has not yet finished making? For most of the life of corporation tax the answer was simple. You made the profit, you closed the books, and months later you paid. Then the rules changed for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2019. The very largest companies were told to pay inside the year itself. A company with a calendar year end now hands over the first quarter of its tax bill on 14 March, when nine months of the trading that will produce it have not yet happened.

That rule, and the machinery around it, is the subject of this chapter. Corporation tax for a larger company is not one event a year. It is a calendar. Instalments fall due every quarter. Returns fall due a year after the accounts close. HMRC’s enquiry window stays open longer for a company in a large group than for a company on its own. Discovery can reach back 4, 6 or 20 years. And every one of those dates carries a price when it is missed, in interest or in penalties.

This is the third chapter of Part One. CT self-assessment, the charge to CT and accounting periods, disclosure and discovery, penalties and interest, and CTA 2010 Part 22 (which includes the Chapter 4 surrender of tax refunds) are all core (grade 1) on the 2026 LCG grid. The Living Law (TKS), chapter 5, built the compliance machine for a single invented company, Calder Valve Engineering Ltd, paying four equal instalments. Here we put Calder into a group, and the machine starts to behave differently. The law throughout is FY2026 (1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027).

Abbreviations used in this chapter. Sch 18 = FA 1998 Sch 18 (company returns); TMA = Taxes Management Act 1970; the QIP Regulations = Corporation Tax (Instalment Payments) Regulations 1998, SI 1998/3175; CTA 2009 / CTA 2010; QIP = quarterly instalment payment; AP = accounting period; POA = period of account; RDEC = research and development expenditure credit.

The accounting period, again.

Every date in this chapter hangs from one idea, the accounting period (CTA 2009 ss 9–12; recapped from TKS chapter 20). An AP begins when a company comes within the charge to CT, or when its previous AP ends. It ends on the first of these events:

  • 12 months after it began;
  • the company’s accounting date, or the end of a period for which it makes up accounts;
  • the company starting or ceasing to trade, or coming within or ceasing to be within the charge to CT;
  • the company ceasing to be UK resident (chapter 22);
  • the start of a winding up, or the company entering administration (CTA 2009 ss 10, 12; chapter 14).

What is missing from the list: a change of owner. When our invented group, Tarnmoor, buys Calder on 1 April GY1, Calder’s AP simply begins as usual that day, because its old year ended on 31 March. When Tarnmoor buys Brackenwell Sensors Ltd on 1 July GY2, Brackenwell’s AP runs straight on to 31 December GY2. The acquisition matters enormously for losses (chapter 14), group relief (chapter 15) and the associated company count (below). It does not reset the tax calendar.

The running case. Tarnmoor plc is an invented, widely held, London-listed engineering group. Every company, person and number in its story is invented for teaching. Its story years are Group Years (GY1, GY2, …), never calendar years, and every computation applies FY2026 law. Short forms: TPLC (Tarnmoor plc), TEL (Tarnmoor Engineering Ltd), TES (Tarnmoor Estates Ltd), TFL (Tarnmoor Finance Ltd), CVE (Calder), BSL (Brackenwell).

Long and short periods. The 12-month ceiling creates the long period problem. A company may make up accounts for 15 months, for example on a change of year end or in its first period. Tax cannot follow: the first 12 months form one AP and the last 3 months a second. Two returns, two computations, two payment dates, from one set of accounts. A short POA (such as the 9 months Calder uses in GY3 to move its year end) is one AP, and every threshold in it is scaled by 9/12.

Notification. A company must notify HMRC that it has come within the charge to CT within 3 months after the start of its first AP (FA 2004 s 55). A company chargeable for an AP that has not received a notice to deliver a return must notify chargeability within 12 months after the AP ends (Sch 18 para 2). Failure to notify is penalised under FA 2008 Sch 41, geared to the potential lost revenue and the company’s behaviour. In a large group the risk lies with newcomers: the hive-down vehicle, the new holding company formed for a deal. The group tax function keeps an entity list and adds every new company the day it is incorporated.

When the return is due.

The return is built on the accounts, so its deadline is built on the accounts too. Sch 18 para 14 sets the filing date as the last of:

Date Applies
(a) 12 months after the end of the AP for which the return is made always
(b) 12 months after the end of the relevant POA POA of 18 months or less
(b) 30 months after the start of the relevant POA POA longer than 18 months
(c) 3 months after the notice to deliver the return always

The “relevant period of account” is the POA in which the AP’s last day falls (para 14(2)). Put simply, the filing date follows the period of account: the point that decided marks in N25 Q4 (administration of a new subsidiary).

Worked example 3.1: a 15-month first period (labelled illustration, not part of the story)

A new subsidiary starts trading on 1 October (Year A) and makes up its first accounts for 15 months to 31 December (Year B). Assume it is outside the QIP regime and in a large (not small) group.

AP 1 AP 2
Period 1 Oct Year A – 30 Sep Year B (12 months) 1 Oct – 31 Dec Year B (3 months)
Normal payment date (9 months + 1 day after the AP end; TMA s 59D) 1 July Year C 1 October Year C
Filing date (Sch 18 para 14: 12 months after the end of a POA of up to 18 months) 31 December Year C 31 December Year C
Enquiry window closes (large group: 12 months from the filing date, Sch 18 para 24) 31 December Year D 31 December Year D
Ordinary discovery limit (4 years after the AP end, para 46) 30 September Year F 31 December Year F

AP 1’s return gets 15 months, not 12; its enquiry window runs 27 months from its own year end. Both returns must be delivered by the same day; the tax for AP 1 is due six months before that.

The trap: payment does not follow the period of account. For a company outside the instalment rules, the tax for each AP is due 9 months and 1 day after that AP ends (TMA s 59D). The law lets the paperwork wait for the accounts, but not the money: profit can be estimated, finished accounts cannot be rushed.

In a group, the return is where the group regimes are switched on. Group relief claims and surrenders, and many elections and claims, are made in or with the return of the company concerned. Each of Tarnmoor’s UK companies files its own return with its own filing date; the tax function’s real deadline is the earliest of them, because a surrender in one company’s return must match a claim in another’s (chapter 15).

Exam lens: accounting periods and filing dates - Grade: the charge to CT and accounting periods 1; CT self-assessment 1. - Past appearances: N25 Q4 (20 marks, 4/8/8; part (a) admin on incorporation: notification, APs, “the filing date is based on the period of account”); M25 Q6 (10 marks, 5/5; a 15-month POA shifting filing and enquiry dates, answered poorly). - Traps: moving the payment date with the filing date; forgetting that a long POA gives two APs with the same filing date; treating an acquisition as ending an AP. - Layout: a short table of APs with payment date, filing date, enquiry window close and discovery limits, each as a full date.

Paying before the bill is known.

History. Quarterly instalments arrived with CT self-assessment, for APs ending on or after 1 July 1999 (SI 1998/3175), and were phased in. HMRC’s COTAX manual (COM95005) records that 60% of a large company’s liability went through instalments for APs ending 1 July 1999 to 30 June 2000, 72% for the next year, 88% for the year after, and 100% for APs ending on or after 1 July 2002. The effect was to bring large companies’ tax forward, closer to the time the profits were earned. The very large company regime, inserted by SI 2017/1072, applies to APs beginning on or after 1 April 2019 (CTM92520).

Analogy. Paying the bill while the meal is still being eaten: a large company pays for two courses before the meal ends and two shortly after; a very large company pays the whole bill before it puts down its fork.

The rules (SI 1998/3175 reg 3, as substituted).

Large company Very large company
Test Augmented profits > £1.5m Augmented profits > £20m
Instalments (12-month AP) 14th day of months 7, 10, 13, 16 from the start of the AP 14th day of months 3, 6, 9, 12
Calendar-year AP 14 July, 14 October, 14 January, 14 April 14 March, 14 June, 14 September, 14 December
Amount of each instalment 3/n × total liability (n = months in the AP, maximum 12) same
Thresholds ÷ (1 + associated companies); × months/12 for a short AP same
Year of grace Not large if profits ≤ £10m (also divided) and not large in the previous 12 months (reg 3(5)) None: very large in the first AP in which the threshold is exceeded (CTM92520, CTM92800)
De minimis Not large if total liability ≤ £10,000 (pro rata for a short AP) (reg 3(4)) —

Augmented profits are TTP plus exempt distributions received, other than those from companies in the recipient’s own group (TKS chapter 20 recap). Calder held no shareholdings, so its augmented profits equal its TTP.

The misconception: “a company always gets a year’s grace before instalments”. The grace is for large companies only. HMRC’s manual is explicit that the CTM92530 period of grace does not apply in deciding whether a company is very large. There is no warning year.

Counting the family.

The thresholds are divided by one plus the number of associated companies and scaled down for a short AP. Since 1 April 2023 the associated company test is control (CTA 2010 ss 18E–18J, as recapped from TKS chapter 20): companies are associated if one controls the other or both are under the control of the same person or persons. Dormant companies and passive holding companies are disregarded; non-UK companies count.

When do you count? Two different answers.

Purpose When associates are counted Authority
Small profits rate and marginal relief Associated at any time in the AP (even for part of it) CTA 2010 s 18E; CTM03580
QIP thresholds (£1.5m, £20m, £10m) As at the day before the AP begins (or on its first day if the day before was not in an AP) HMRC’s reading of SI 1998/3175 reg 3: CTM92530

So the same acquisition has two timings. Join a group and your marginal relief limits are divided at once, for the whole AP in which you join; your instalment thresholds are divided only from the next AP that begins after you joined. The logic is practical: a very large company’s first instalment falls in month 3, so it must know its regime at the start of the year. Status: this is HMRC’s manual; the regulation’s current text was not opened for this chapter (see the notes). In an exam, cite reg 3 and HMRC’s reading.

Worked example 3.2: Tarnmoor’s thresholds (invented)

Company / AP Counting date Associates Divisor Large threshold (£) Very large threshold (£) £10m grace limit (£)
31 December companies, GY1 31 Dec before GY1 (TPLC, TEL, TES, TFL, TWS, TVS, TCM, TIL) 7 8 187,500 2,500,000 1,250,000
31 December companies, GY2 31 Dec GY1 (+ Calder) 8 9 166,667 2,222,222 1,111,111
31 December companies, GY3 and GY4 31 Dec GY2 / GY3 (+ Brackenwell) 9 10 150,000 2,000,000 1,000,000
Calder, AP 1 Apr GY1 – 31 Mar GY2 31 Mar GY1 (owned by the Oldroyd family, who own no other companies) 0 1 1,500,000 20,000,000 10,000,000
Calder, AP 1 Apr GY2 – 31 Mar GY3 31 Mar GY2 (Brackenwell joins 1 July GY2: too late) 8 9 166,667 2,222,222 1,111,111
Calder, 9-month AP 1 Apr – 31 Dec GY3 31 Mar GY3 9 10 112,500 (× 9/12) 1,500,000 (× 9/12) 750,000 (× 9/12)

Tarnmoor Pumps Ltd (dormant) never counts. For marginal relief the divisors are (GY1 9, because Calder is associated for part of GY1; GY2 10; GY3 10): irrelevant in practice, since every trading company is far above £250,000. Every main trading company is far above every QIP threshold too, so conclusions do not change; but the divisor and the counting date earn the marks.

Calder joins the group.

The Living Law, chapter 5: in its year to 31 March 2027, Calder was a standalone company with TTP £2,000,000, no associated companies, CT £500,000, paid as a large company (large in the prior year, so no grace) in four instalments of £125,000 on 14 October 2026, 14 January, 14 April and 14 July 2027.

Some years later, in our invented story, TPLC buys Calder from the Oldroyd family on 1 April GY1 for £32m. Calder keeps its 31 March year end for now. Graham Pike, Calder’s finance director, asks Tom Hesketh, Tarnmoor’s head of tax, whether Calder is now very large: eight associates, forecast profits £3.0m, and £20m ÷ 9 = £2,222,222.

Worked example 3.3: Calder’s first two group APs (invented)

AP 1 April GY1 – 31 March GY2

£
Taxable total profits (including taxable RDEC £400,000) = augmented profits 3,000,000
Divisor for QIPs (associates counted at 31 March GY1) 1
Large threshold £1,500,000: exceeded? Yes
Very large threshold £20,000,000: exceeded? No
Year of grace? (large in the previous 12 months) No
CT at 25% 750,000
Less RDEC set off at step 1 (chapter 10), given effect in the return (400,000)
Net CT for the AP 350,000

Instalments. HMRC’s view (CIRD89870) is that the RDEC is not taken into account when computing QIPs; it is claimed in the return. So the instalments are 3/12 × £750,000:

Due date Month of AP £
14 October GY1 7 187,500
14 January GY2 10 187,500
14 April GY2 13 187,500
14 July GY2 16 187,500
Total 750,000

The £400,000 of credit is recovered once the return is filed and the claim made; CIRD89870 says the credit may then be used to discharge later QIPs. Calder files its return early, in summer GY2, so the credit goes towards its next AP’s instalments.

AP 1 April GY2 – 31 March GY3. Associates counted at 31 March GY2: 8; divisor 9; very large threshold £2,222,222. Calder’s forecast profits are comfortably above it (the AP’s figures are fixed in later chapters), so Calder is very large (no grace): instalments on 14 June GY2, 14 September GY2, 14 December GY2 and 14 March GY3.

Calder’s instalment dates in calendar GY2: 14 January, 14 April, 14 July (AP to 31 March GY2) and 14 June, 14 September, 14 December (AP to 31 March GY3): six instalments in twelve months.

Going further: acquisitions and the instalment calendar - Diligence point: on any acquisition, establish the target’s QIP status for its current AP (its own history, not the buyer’s divisor) and the date its first very large instalment will fall once the group’s associates count. - Cash: a company moving from large to very large pays six (or more) instalments in the transition year. Treasury needs the dates before the first is due. - Merged R&D scheme: the RDEC raises TTP (it is taxable) but does not reduce QIPs, so it can tip a company into instalments and increases the cash paid in the year. Filing early lets the credit discharge the next AP’s QIPs.

Exam lens: instalments - Grade: CT self-assessment 1; penalties and interest 1. - Past appearances: M25 Q2 (15 marks, 10/5): very large company instalments with changing forecasts, done badly (“forecast changes were not trued up, and some candidates did not know the very large company rules”); N24 Q5 (20 marks): a US group buys a UK SME: filing and instalments now that the company is in a large group, thresholds divided, payment dates (4 marks); quarterly instalments also appear as the tail of a full computation in N25 Q1. - Style: compute the threshold (show the divisor and the counting date), state the regime, list every due date in full, then the amounts. - Traps: months counted from the start of the AP; very large has no grace; the £10m grace limit is divided too; the RDEC does not reduce QIPs; short APs scale the thresholds and change the number of instalments.

Truing up.

An instalment is judged afterwards. Once the final liability is settled, each instalment “should have been” 3/n of it, and interest runs on any shortfall from each due date until it is paid (or until the normal due date, after which ordinary late payment interest applies). The company’s duty is to pay on its best estimate and to correct as the estimate moves: if the forecast rises, the next instalment catches up so that the cumulative total matches what should by then have been paid on the new forecast; if it falls, the company can claim back an overpayment (reg 6). The examiners’ M25 Q2 comment is the warning: forecast changes were not trued up.

Worked example 3.4: truing up (labelled illustration, not part of the story)

A very large company with a calendar year forecasts a liability of £4.0m in March and June, £6.0m in September; the final liability is £6.4m. QIP debit interest 6.25%.

Due date Forecast (£) Cumulative due on forecast (£) Paid (£) Cumulative paid (£) Should have been, on final £6.4m (£) Shortfall (£) Interest to next date, 3 months at 6.25% (£)
14 March 4,000,000 1,000,000 1,000,000 1,000,000 1,600,000 600,000 9,375.00
14 June 4,000,000 2,000,000 1,000,000 2,000,000 3,200,000 1,200,000 18,750.00
14 September 6,000,000 4,500,000 2,500,000 4,500,000 4,800,000 300,000 4,687.50
14 December 6,400,000 6,400,000 1,900,000 6,400,000 6,400,000 nil nil
Total 6,400,000 32,812.50

Honest forecasting avoids penalties, not interest. (Interest simplified to three-month blocks; HMRC computes it daily.)

Penalty. Reg 13 allows a penalty where a company knowingly or recklessly pays too little by instalments (EM8330’s description) (or makes a fraudulent or negligent repayment claim). The maximum is twice the interest on the shortfall (EM8330). HMRC’s manual adds that a penalty arises only after the return has been filed and the normal due date has passed (COM95070). In the example above, had the March and June instalments been deliberately low, the maximum would be £65,625.

Short APs for very large companies (CTM92815). Where the AP ends on the last day of a month, the final instalment is due on the 14th of that last month; the first is due 2 months and 13 days after the AP starts; later ones at 3-month intervals; an instalment date that would fall on or after the final date drops out, the liability being spread over the remaining dates.

Worked example 3.5: Calder’s 9-month AP, 1 April – 31 December GY3 (invented)

Associates at 31 March GY3 9 (divisor 10)
Very large threshold £20m ÷ 10 × 9/12 = £1,500,000
First instalment 1 April + 2 months 13 days = 14 June GY3
Second 14 September GY3
Third (would be 14 December = the final date) 14 December GY3 (final)
Amount of each 3/9 = one third of the total liability

The June instalment rests on a trading forecast. On 15 June Calder announces the closure of its process valves division (restructuring provision £1.8m), and on 1 October it sells the business to Tarnmoor Vallaria SA (TVS, in the invented country of Vallaria) for £6.0m of intangible assets (a taxable realisation credit; chapter 11) and £1.4m of plant. Neither was in the June forecast; the December instalment carries the catch-up and interest runs on the earlier shortfalls. Calder’s TTP for this AP is computed in later chapters; this chapter fixes only the dates and the threshold.

The tax function’s lesson: a known transaction belongs in the forecast as soon as it is probable, not when it completes.

Paying as a family.

Each company is a separate taxpayer with its own instalments, and that separateness costs money: one company overpays and earns 3.50%, another underpays and is charged 6.25%. Two tools close the gap.

Group payment arrangements (TMA s 59F). HMRC may agree that one company pays CT on behalf of members of its group. The group is a company and its 51% subsidiaries (and theirs). The nominated company must be UK resident; members must have the same accounting date and be up to date with filing and payments; and the liability stays with each company (GOV.UK, “Corporation Tax: group payment arrangements”). The arrangement changes who writes the cheque, not who owes the tax. HMRC’s guidance describes a single payment on each due date by the nominated company, allocated among the members once their liabilities are known: one member’s overpayment covers another’s shortfall from the day it was paid.

In our invented case Tom Hesketh sets up a group payment arrangement from GY3 for the 31 December companies, with TFL as nominated company. Calder cannot join while its year ends on 31 March: one reason for its 9-month AP in GY3. From GY4 it has a calendar year and joins.

Surrender of tax refunds within a group (CTA 2010 Part 22 Ch 4, ss 963–966). A group company due a tax refund for an AP may surrender all or part of it to another member of the same group (s 963(1)). Conditions:

  • the group is the 75% group relief group (COM122020);
  • both companies have the same AP, and are members of the group from the start of that AP until the notice;
  • the companies give a joint notice to HMRC before the refund is made.

QIP Regulations reg 9 extends the rule to instalment overpayments so that the recipient is treated as having paid the surrendered tax on the dates the surrendering company actually paid it: the debit/credit interest differential is neutralised (CTM92740). Payments between the companies for the surrender are dealt with by s 966.

Worked example 3.6: TES surrenders a refund to TEL, GY2 (invented)

Both companies are very large in GY2 (divisor 9; threshold £2,222,222) and pay on 14 March, 14 June, 14 September and 14 December GY2. No group payment arrangement exists yet.

TES (£) TEL (£)
Final CT for GY2 (forecast included the depot gain; sale slipped to 30 April GY3) 2,226,250
Overpaid / (underpaid) in total 569,375 (tax at 25% on the expected £2,277,500 gain) (400,000)
Per instalment 142,343.75 over 100,000 short
Refund surrendered (joint notice before repayment) (400,000) +400,000
Repaid to TES 169,375 —

TEL paid four instalments of £456,562.50 (£1,826,250) on an early forecast; a stronger second half took its liability to £2,226,250. Because TES’s overpayment on each date (£142,343.75) exceeds TEL’s shortfall on that date (£100,000), reg 9 leaves TEL with no QIP shortfall at any date.

Interest saved (simplified): assume that without the surrender TEL’s shortfalls and TES’s overpayments would each have been settled on the normal due date, 1 October GY3; months to the nearest month from each instalment date: 19, 16, 13 and 10 (58 in total).

£
TEL’s QIP debit interest avoided: £100,000 × 6.25% × 58/12 30,208
TES’s credit interest forgone: £100,000 × 3.50% × 58/12 (16,917)
Net saving to the group (before tax effects) 13,291

Rule of thumb: £400,000 × (6.25% − 3.50%) = £11,000 a year.

Exam lens: group payment arrangements and refund surrenders - Grade: CT self-assessment 1; Part 22 CTA 2010 (excluding Chs 3 and 8 and ss 990–995) 1. - Traps: the GPA group is 51% with the same accounting date, the refund surrender group is the 75% group relief group with the same AP; the surrender notice must precede the refund; a GPA does not transfer liability.

The enquiry window.

HMRC may open an enquiry into a return only by giving notice within a window (Sch 18 para 24):

Return Enquiry window
Delivered on or before the filing date, company not in a group, or in a small group 12 months after the day the return was delivered
Delivered on or before the filing date by a member of a group that is not a small group (Companies Act 2006 ss 383, 474) 12 months after the filing date
Delivered late, or amended To the quarter day after the first anniversary of the day of delivery (or amendment)

Large groups file early; without the group rule, early filing would shorten HMRC’s time to look. With it, filing early buys a large group nothing in finality. Each return has its own window; once notice is given in time, the enquiry itself can run on well beyond it.

M25 Q6 combined the rules: a company in a large group with a 15-month POA. Candidates applied the small-company limits and missed the long period. In worked example 3.1, both returns are due 31 December Year C and both windows close 31 December Year D: for AP 1, 27 months after its own year end.

The story. Calder’s return for its 9-month AP to 31 December GY3 is due by 31 December GY4. Calder is in a large group, so the window runs to 31 December GY5, however early it files. On 1 June GY5 HMRC opens an enquiry into the price of the GY3 sale to TVS (chapter 27).

An enquiry ends with a closure notice stating HMRC’s conclusions and making any amendments to the return; the company can appeal. The tax function’s best defence is the file built when the return was prepared: computations, reasoning on uncertain points, the evidence behind transfer prices.

Discovery.

Once the window has closed, the return is normally final; the exception is a discovery assessment where HMRC discovers that tax has been lost (profits omitted, relief excessive). Sch 18 para 46 time limits run from the end of the AP:

Behaviour Time limit
Ordinary 4 years
Loss of tax brought about carelessly 6 years
Brought about deliberately; failure to notify chargeability; certain DOTAS failures (including failure to notify a scheme reference number) 20 years

For a delivered return the statute also protects the company: in broad terms, a discovery assessment needs careless or deliberate conduct, or a loss of tax that an officer could not reasonably have been expected to be aware of from the information made available before the window closed (Sch 18 discovery provisions, paras 41 onwards). Hence the practice of disclosing contentious positions in or with the return: full disclosure narrows the door through which discovery can come.

Misconception: “once the enquiry window closes, we are safe”. Safe from an enquiry, not from discovery. Discovery needs something new or something hidden; an enquiry needs no reason at all.

Worked example 3.7: Calder’s 9-month AP to 31 December GY3 (invented)

Limit Last date for a discovery assessment
Ordinary (4 years) 31 December GY7
Careless (6 years) 31 December GY9
Deliberate (20 years) 31 December GY23

Records. A company must keep the records needed to deliver a correct return; failure can cost up to £3,000 per AP (Sch 18 para 23). In a group, “records” also means TP documentation (chapter 27) and the reasoning behind each judgement; the UTT notification (chapter 4) shares the same logic of telling HMRC early.

Exam lens: enquiries and discovery - Grade: disclosure and discovery 1; CT self-assessment 1. - Past appearances: M25 Q6 (10 marks, 5/5: large group enquiry windows with a 15-month POA; discovery for careless behaviour; poor); M24 Q3 (15 marks; part (c) 3 marks on HMRC enquiry/discovery on a loss return). - Traps: small-group time limits applied to a large group; ignoring the long POA; counting discovery limits from the filing date rather than the AP end.

Late, wrong or silent.

Late filing: flat-rate penalties (Sch 18 para 17, as amended by FA 2026 s 265). For returns with a filing date on or after 1 April 2026:

Failure Within 3 months after the filing date Otherwise
Late return £200 (was £100) £400 (was £200)
Third successive failure (liable to a fixed penalty for each of the two preceding periods) £1,000 (was £500) £2,000 (was £1,000)

The statute says £200 then £400 in total (GOV.UK’s “another £200” means the same). FA 2026 s 265 also lets HMRC change the amounts by regulations.

Real-calendar illustration (labelled): year ended 31 March 2025 → filing date 31 March 2026 → old amounts; year ended 30 April 2025 → filing date 30 April 2026 → new amounts.

Late filing: tax-geared penalties (Sch 18 para 18). If the return is not delivered within 18 months after the end of the AP (or by the filing date if later): 10% of the tax unpaid at that time; 20% if delivered more than 2 years after the AP end.

Story: Brackenwell’s third return (invented). At completion on 1 July GY2, Brackenwell’s return for its year to 31 December GY1 is still unfiled. It carries the ERIS payable credit claim of £943,950 (chapter 10). Its two previous returns, from before the story, were both late, so the next late return would be a third successive failure: £1,000, or £2,000 if more than 3 months late. Tom Hesketh’s team files well before the filing date, 31 December GY2. The amount is small; the signal to HMRC about a newly acquired company’s controls is not.

Inaccuracy (FA 2007 Sch 24). Careless or deliberate inaccuracies in a return: maximum 30% (careless), 70% (deliberate), 100% (deliberate and concealed) of the potential lost revenue, reduced for disclosure.

Failure to notify (FA 2008 Sch 41). Penalties for failing to notify chargeability, geared to the potential lost revenue and behaviour.

Interest (rates in force when this chapter was written; they move with Bank Rate).

Rate From
Late payment interest (Bank Rate + 4%) 7.75% 9 January 2026
Repayment interest (Bank Rate − 1%, minimum 0.5%) 2.75% 9 January 2026
QIP underpayments (Bank Rate + 2.5%) 6.25% 29 December 2025
QIP overpayments (Bank Rate − 0.25%) 3.50% 29 December 2025

The margins over Bank Rate for QIP underpayments and late payment rose on 6 April 2025 (from + 1% and + 2.5%); Bank Rate has been 3.75% since 18 December 2025.

Late payment penalty pending further appeal (FA 2026 s 264). FA 2009 Sch 56 item 18 is extended to amounts payable under TMA s 56(3)(b), tax due after a tribunal decision while a further appeal is pending, for amounts payable on or after 1 April 2026. A group that loses at the tribunal and appeals further can no longer sit on the tax without that risk.

Exam lens: penalties and interest - Grade: penalties and interest on under/overpayments/failure to notify etc 1. - Traps: using the pre-FA 2026 amounts (an FA 2026 sitting will expect £200/£400 and £1,000/£2,000); describing the persistent penalty as an extra £1,000 on top; forgetting the tax-geared 10%/20%; treating QIP interest as a penalty.

The rest of the calendar.

Returns and instalments are the spine of the calendar, but a large group’s year is crowded with other dates, each owned by its own chapter:

Obligation Chapter
R&D claim notification (first claim, or first for 3 years: within 6 months after the POA ends) and the additional information form 10
Interest restriction return and reporting company 28
Pillar Two registration, GloBE information return and top-up tax returns 30
Country-by-country report; TP master file and local file 27
SAO notification and certificate; tax strategy; uncertain tax treatment notification 4

Going further: three planning choices 1. The accounting date of an acquired company. Leaving Calder on 31 March kept it out of the group payment arrangement and gave the tax function two calendars. The 9-month AP aligned it but created a forecasting problem. A long POA instead (up to 18 months) would have pushed the filing date out but not the payment dates. 2. Cash. Joining a group moves a company from large to very large one AP later (on HMRC’s counting date); treasury needs the six-instalment year in the forecast. 3. Interest management. A group payment arrangement, refund surrenders made before the refund is paid, and forecasts updated before each instalment are worth real money in a group the size of Tarnmoor. None changes a pound of tax; all change what the tax costs.

A typical Tarnmoor year (invented): 31 December companies pay through the GPA on 14 March, June, September and December; Calder (until GY4) runs its own calendar; returns are due by 31 December after the year, with group relief claims and surrenders lined up across them; every new company enters the calendar on the day it arrives, with its own counting date for associates and its own history of late returns.

How the examiner tests it.

Administration is a regular 10–15 mark question or the tail of a computation (compliance and governance appeared in N23 Q5, M25 Q3, M25 Q6, M24 Q3(c), N24 Q5, N25 Q4(a), M26 Q1(a), N23 Q1(b)).

  • M25 Q2 (15 marks, 10/5): CT computation then very large instalments with changing forecasts: badly done (no truing up; very large rules unknown).
  • M25 Q6 (10 marks, 5/5): enquiry windows for a large-group company with a 15-month POA; discovery for careless behaviour: poor (small-group limits applied; long period missed).
  • N24 Q5 (20 marks): UK compliance after a US group buys a UK SME: filing and QIPs now that the company is in a large group (4 marks), alongside CbC, TP, CIR and stamp duty.
  • N25 Q4 (20 marks, 4/8/8): admin on incorporation of a new subsidiary: notification, APs, the filing date following the POA.

Style: technical prose and computation; no letter or report format; 0.5–1 mark per point, so state each date, threshold and conclusion separately; the rubric wants workings to the nearest month and pound, so give full dates. Layout: threshold working (limit ÷ divisor × months/12) → regime → table of due dates and amounts → truing up and interest. Where the question says “administrative obligations”: notification, filing, payment, enquiry, then penalties for each.

What to take away.

An AP lasts at most 12 months; a 15-month POA gives two APs and two returns; a change of ownership does not end an AP. The filing date follows the POA; payment (9 months and 1 day after each AP, outside QIPs) does not. Large (> £1.5m) pay in months 7, 10, 13, 16; very large (> £20m) in months 3, 6, 9, 12; both divided by 1 + associates and scaled for short APs; for QIPs, HMRC counts associates at the day before the AP begins. Large companies have a year of grace (≤ £10m, divided; not large before); very large have none; no QIPs if the liability is £10,000 or less. True up when forecasts change; interest 6.25%/3.50%; penalties only for knowing or reckless underpayment (up to twice the interest); the RDEC does not reduce QIPs. GPAs (51%, same accounting date) and refund surrenders (75%, same AP, joint notice before the refund) cut the interest cost. Enquiry window: 12 months from delivery, but from the filing date for a company in a group that is not small. Discovery: 4/6/20 years from the AP end. Late filing: £200/£400; £1,000/£2,000 for a third successive failure; 10%/20% tax-geared.

The calendar tells a group when to pay and when to file. The next chapter asks who answers for it: the senior accounting officer, the board that publishes a tax strategy, and the rules that make large groups tell HMRC what they are unsure about.
