Chapter twenty five: Outbound: branch or subsidiary.

A choice that may not last.

On 13 July 2026 HMRC published draft legislation that would take away the choice this chapter is about. For fifteen years a UK company with a branch abroad has been able to decide whether that branch’s profits and losses stay inside UK corporation tax or fall outside it. The draft would make the foreign branch exemption compulsory for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027. A policy paper published on 21 May 2026 had explained the aim: it was directed at companies using the losses and capital allowances of foreign branches to reduce their UK profits.

That draft is proposed, not law. The 2027 sittings test Finance Act 2026, and under that Act the exemption is still an election. So the old question is still the live one, and it is one of the oldest in international tax: when a company goes abroad, should it go as itself, through a branch, or through a new company, a subsidiary? And if it goes as itself, should it ask to have the branch taken out of the UK tax base?

This is chapter 25, the fourth chapter of Part Four (crossing borders). Overseas branches and subsidiaries sit inside the core (grade 1) grid row “Company residence and chargeable profits of non-UK resident companies and concept of permanent establishment/branch”. Company distributions received (foreign dividends) and unremittable income are core. “Transfers concerning companies of different member States” and international movements of capital are non-core (grade 2). The Living Law (TKS), chapter 26, introduced the branch and the subsidiary, the s 18A election and its opening negative amount, the dividend exemption and s 140. Here we take each to Advanced Technical depth.

Statutes: Corporation Tax Act 2009 (CTA 2009: Part 2 Ch 3A, ss 18A–18S; Part 9A, ss 931A–931S; ss 173–175; Part 18, ss 1274–1278); Taxation (International and Other Provisions) Act 2010 (TIOPA 2010: Part 2, double tax relief); Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992 (TCGA 1992: ss 140–140L); Finance Act 2009 s 37 and Sch 17. The law throughout is that for FY2026.

Two ways to go abroad.

A UK resident company is chargeable to corporation tax on all its profits wherever they arise (CTA 2009 s 5). A branch is not a separate person: it is the company itself doing business in another country, so its profits are the company’s profits and sit in its UK computation, whatever tax the other country also charges.

A subsidiary is a new company with its own legal personality. If it is incorporated and managed abroad it is not UK resident, and the UK does not tax its profits as they arise. Chapter 22 explained how residence follows central management and control: a foreign subsidiary whose real decisions are taken in Leeds can find itself resident in Leeds, defeating the purpose of creating it.

The Living Law’s picture: a branch is a spare room in your own house; a subsidiary is a separate flat you own. The spare room is part of the household accounts. The flat has its own meter, bills and tenancy, and money comes back to you only when the flat pays you something.

The territorial turn. For most of the last century the UK taxed both routes on a credit basis: branch profits as they arose, dividends from foreign subsidiaries when received, with credit for foreign tax. Then:

Date Change
1 July 2009 Foreign dividends broadly exempt (CTA 2009 Part 9A); onshore pooling and EUFT repealed; ICTA 1988 s 765 Treasury consent replaced by reporting (FA 2009 Sch 17)
19 July 2011 Foreign branch exemption election (CTA 2009 Part 2 Ch 3A, inserted by FA 2011 Sch 13)
2012–2013 Reformed CFC regime (FA 2012 Sch 20; CFC APs beginning on or after 1 January 2013); branch anti-diversion rule aligned with it
2026 FA 2026: s 18S updated to the OECD Model approved on 18 November 2025 (otherwise no change to Ch 3A or Part 9A)
13 July 2026 Draft Finance Bill 2026-27 clauses: compulsory exemption (proposed, not law)

The UK moved from taxing foreign profits with credit to leaving most of them alone, while building tools (CFCs, the branch anti-diversion rule, transfer pricing) to stop profits being diverted from home.

So a company going abroad has three possible positions, not two: (1) a branch taxed in the UK with credit; (2) a branch exempted by election; (3) a subsidiary whose profits come home as exempt dividends.

The branch taxed as part of the company.

Without an election, the branch is part of the company’s business. If the company trades in the UK and carries out a contract abroad through a permanent establishment (PE), the foreign profits and losses are part of one trading computation. The other country taxes the profits attributable to the PE as its treaty allows (chapters 23–24); the UK taxes them again and gives credit.

Two consequences:

  1. A branch loss reduces UK tax at once, against the company’s other profits of the same period.
  2. A profitable branch never pays less than the UK rate overall. Credit tops foreign tax up to UK tax; it never refunds foreign tax that is higher.

Chapter 24 set out the credit limit (TIOPA 2010 s 42: R × IG, source by source, after allocating deductions under s 52). For trade income, the credit cannot exceed the CT attributable to the income from the particular transaction, arrangement or asset, after a just and reasonable share of deductions (s 44). Two refinements for branches:

  • Carry forward and back of unrelieved foreign tax on a PE’s profits: forward, or back to APs beginning up to 3 years earlier, against UK tax on the same PE’s profits (ss 72–78).
  • Foreign use of branch losses (ss 71A–71B, FA 2018): where a PE loss is used abroad against other persons’ profits (for example in a foreign group consolidation), the foreign tax available for credit on the PE’s later profits is reduced by the tax saved.

Calder’s Vallarian branch (invented). Our invented group, Tarnmoor (everything about it is invented for teaching), bought Calder Valve Engineering Ltd (CVE; 31 March year end) on 1 April GY1. In August GY2 Calder began an installation contract at a refinery in Vallaria (invented; CT rate 20%). The project ran 14 months, to September GY3. The invented UK–Vallaria treaty treats a construction or installation project lasting more than 12 months as a PE (chapter 24). So Calder had a Vallarian branch from the start.

Worked example 25.1: Calder’s branch without an election (invented)

Vallarian loss relief is ignored (story simplification: in real life Vallaria would probably carry the GY3 loss forward and tax less of the later profit).

£ AP 1 Apr GY2 – 31 Mar GY3 9-month AP 1 Apr – 31 Dec GY3 Project life
PE result included in Calder’s trading profits (300,000) 900,000 600,000
UK CT at 25% on the PE result (75,000) 225,000 150,000
Vallarian tax at 20% — 180,000 180,000
Credit limit (s 42/s 44: UK tax on the contract’s income) — 225,000
DTR credit (lower of foreign tax and limit) — (180,000) (180,000)
UK tax (relief) attributable to the PE (75,000) 45,000 (30,000)
Total tax: Vallaria + UK 150,000

£150,000 ÷ £600,000 = 25.0%. Without an election a branch is taxed at the UK rate on its net result, with Vallaria taking its share first.

The election.

CTA 2009 s 18A: where a UK resident company has elected, exemption adjustments are made in calculating its taxable total profits so that the profits and losses of its foreign PEs are left out. The symmetry is the price.

Mechanics (s 18A(4)–(7)). For each relevant foreign territory (one in which the company carries on, or has carried on, business through a PE) there is a relevant profits amount or a relevant losses amount. The foreign permanent establishments amount = aggregate relevant profits amounts − aggregate relevant losses amounts. It may be positive or negative, and the exemption adjustments remove it either way.

Measuring the branch profit.

Situation Measure Source
Full treaty territory (treaty with a non-discrimination article covering PEs: s 18R) Profits the treaty’s business profits article would attribute to the PE s 18A; INTM281040
No full treaty Profits that would be attributed under a treaty in the form of the OECD Model, as defined in s 18S (updated by FA 2026 Sch 7 to the Model approved on 18 November 2025) s 18A, s 18S
Capital allowances Notional allowances (s 18C), given automatically on the most favourable assumptions, so that allowances on exempt PE assets cannot reduce the profits that stay taxable INTM285020 (HMRC’s view)
Leasing Amounts from a lease where the lessor or a connected company claimed UK allowances are left out (s 18C(3)) INTM285050

The edges.

  • Investment business: profits or losses of any part of the business consisting of making investments are left out of the relevant amounts.
  • UK land: UK property business profits and UK land-linked gains are never exempted (s 18A(2A), (2B)).
  • Small companies: only PEs in full treaty territories count.
  • Chargeable gains are generally within the relevant amounts (immovable property abroad used for the PE included: s 18B); but close companies’ gains are excluded (s 18P(2)) unless on assets used solely for the PE’s trade (s 18P(3)), in which case credit relief applies to excluded gains in the normal way.
  • Shipping and air transport in international traffic are excluded.

Interaction.

  • No credit: foreign tax on an exempt relevant profits amount is not “tax payable” for credit (TIOPA 2010 s 18(3A)).
  • UK-to-UK TP exemption: s 164A TIOPA 2010 does not apply where s 18A exemption adjustments are made in relation to the activities (chapter 27).
  • Intangibles: an asset used in an exempt PE cannot pass tax-neutrally within the intangibles group (chapter 11).

All or nothing. The election covers every foreign PE of the company, present and future. It cannot be made branch by branch. A group wanting different answers for different branches must put them in different companies.

Timing (s 18F; INTM281020).

Rule Detail
Effect Applies to all APs beginning on or after the relevant day (s 18F(1)); an AP straddling the relevant day is split (s 18F(4))
Relevant day (UK resident company) The day on which the company’s next AP is expected to begin when the election is made (HMRC: objective, by reference to the normal accounting date); if made before the first AP, the start of that AP (s 18F(2))
Before the relevant day May be revoked by the company (s 18F(6), from 1 January 2013)
After the relevant day Irrevocable; ends automatically only if the company ceases to be UK resident (s 18F(7)–(8))
Change of accounting date The election still takes effect from the original relevant day (HMRC)

Misconception: “electing is a no-brainer once the branch is profitable.” It is not. The election is irrevocable, covers every PE in every country forever, and starts only with the next AP. A company that elects gives up UK relief for every future branch loss. It is a forecast of the whole future pattern of the company’s overseas business, made in advance.

The opening negative amount.

Without a further rule, a company could have branch losses relieved in the UK, then elect just as the branch turned profitable. The transitional matching rules (CTA 2009 ss 18J–18N) close that door.

The look-back (INTM284020). Look back over the 6 years before the first AP the election covers. Aggregate the net losses of all the company’s foreign PEs, net of their profits. Net losses not absorbed by later profits form the total opening negative amount. Chargeable gains and losses are ignored. (A historic extension applies to a “large pre-commencement loss” over £50m in one territory; not needed for the exam.)

Matching (INTM284030). Until the opening negative amount is fully matched by later relevant profits, those profits are not exempt: they stay in charge, with credit relief. Only then does the exemption start.

Streaming (ss 18L–18N; INTM284040). By default the negative amount is one pool across all territories, so a profitable branch in one country can be held in charge by old losses in another. A streaming election attaches amounts to the territory that produced them. It has effect only if the company specifies, in its company tax return for the first relevant AP, how much is to be the streamed opening negative amount for each streamed territory. A streamed amount is reduced only by that territory’s relevant profits (s 18M); unmatched profits elsewhere are treated as unstreamed (s 18N(3)).

The Living Law’s image: the opening negative amount is paying back the rent rebate you enjoyed while the spare room stood empty.

Worked example 25.2: the opening negative amount (labelled, not story)

A company has PEs in two countries, A and B, in the 6 years before its election takes effect.

£ Country A Country B Total
Net results over the 6 years (500,000) 200,000 (300,000)
Total opening negative amount 300,000

The first £300,000 of later relevant profits, from either territory, stays taxable, with credit; only profits above that are exempt. A streaming election (made in the first relevant return) would instead tie the matching to territory A, whose losses produced the amount, so that B’s later profits are not held in charge by A’s history.

Calder’s decision.

When the refinery contract was signed in GY2, Calder’s board compared a branch with a Vallarian subsidiary and chose the branch (below). It did not elect then: the forecast showed early losses, the project was a single contract, and Calder’s engineers expected more installation work abroad as Project Ashlar’s technology sold. An election would have bound every future branch.

In the summer of GY3, with the profit clear, Calder’s finance director, Graham Pike, asked Tom Hesketh, the group head of tax, whether it was too late. It was. Calder was in its 9-month AP (1 April–31 December GY3). An election made then would take effect only from 1 January GY4, after the project had ended: it would exempt nothing and would still bind Calder’s future branches. Calder did not elect.

Worked example 25.3: hindsight: an election made in the AP to 31 March GY3 (labelled counterfactual, not story)

Relevant day: 1 April GY3. Six-year look-back: Vallarian PE loss £300,000 (AP to 31 March GY3): total opening negative amount £300,000.

£ Not exempt (matched) Exempt Total
Relevant profits, 9-month AP to 31 Dec GY3 300,000 600,000 900,000
UK CT at 25% 75,000 — 75,000
Vallarian tax at 20% (apportioned pro rata) 60,000 120,000 180,000
Credit (60,000) not creditable: s 18(3A) (60,000)
UK top-up 15,000 — 15,000
Comparison (£) No election (actual) Election from 1 April GY3
UK relief for GY3 loss (75,000) (75,000)
UK top-up on later profit 45,000 15,000
Vallarian tax 180,000 180,000
Total tax over the project 150,000 120,000
Saving 30,000

Against £30,000: the loss of UK relief at 25% for every future branch loss of Calder, in every country, for ever. For a company about to export a new technology through installation projects that often begin with losses, the board’s view that this was a small prize for a large, permanent commitment is defensible. In an exam, say so as a recommendation.

Guard rails.

The anti-diversion rule (ss 18G–18I). An exemption invites diversion: mobile income (interest, royalties) moved into a low-taxed branch. Since FA 2012 Sch 20 (relevant periods beginning on or after 1 January 2013), the rule is aligned with the CFC regime: in outline, and on HMRC’s description (INTM286010, INTM286310), a PE’s adjusted relevant profits amount (computed without gains) is not exempt so far as it includes profits that would pass through the CFC gateway if the PE were a CFC (s 18H), unless one of the CFC entity exemptions in TIOPA 2010 Part 9A Chs 11–14 (excluded territories, low profits, low profit margin, tax exemption), as adapted, applies (s 18I). The test looks at each AP separately. Pre-2013 periods used an older motive test (not examinable). Chapter 26 teaches the CFC tests.

Reporting. FA 2026 s 48 allows regulations for reporting international controlled transactions (ICTS); the power covers transactions relevant to s 18A exemption adjustments. Regulations are not yet made (chapter 27).

Coming next (proposed, not law). The draft Finance Bill 2026-27 clauses (13 July 2026) would:

  • make the exemption compulsory for APs beginning on or after 1 January 2027, with exceptions including UK property business and investment business;
  • repeal the opening negative amount rules and replace them with transitional rules restricting the carry forward of losses attributable to foreign PEs (income losses, capital losses and capital allowances in separate schedules);
  • apply anti-avoidance to arrangements made on or after 13 July 2026, with a rule against short accounting periods.

These points come from the draft and from professional commentary (KPMG; SWG; Paul Hastings), not from enacted law. Reports differ on whether an earlier start for oil and gas survived into the draft. None of it applies to the 2027 sittings (FA 2026). In practice, check the Bill’s progress.

Exam lens: the branch exemption - Grade: core (within “Company residence … concept of permanent establishment/branch”, 1). - Past appearances: M23 Q2 (15 marks: stay non-exempt, elect, or incorporate; recommend: the examiners reported that some candidates failed to give the recommendation and lost marks; the best answers covered the transitional rules and deferral of the incorporation gain); N25 Q2 (15 marks: PE analysis, then credit relief, the election (timing, irrevocable) and incorporation); M26 Q5 (20 marks: construction PE, branch taxation and DTR, the election and its timing for losses, subsidiary, CMC, CFC, dividend exemption; TP excluded). - Style: explain and compare; short computations of UK tax with and without the election; a recommendation. - Traps: treating the election as per branch; forgetting it starts from the next AP and is irrevocable after the relevant day; ignoring the opening negative amount; giving credit for foreign tax on exempt profits (s 18(3A)); discussing UK residence or migration in a PE question (M26 Q5). - Layout: a short table of UK tax per AP under each option, all in £.

The subsidiary route.

A foreign subsidiary pays foreign tax on its own profits; the UK leaves them alone. Its losses stay with it, for the foreign country’s rules. Its dealings with the UK parent must be at arm’s length (chapter 27), and the CFC rules (chapter 26) stand guard over diverted profits.

Dividends: CTA 2009 Part 9A. Distributions received are charged (s 931A) unless exempt.

Recipient Exempt if Reference
Small company Payer resident only in the UK or a qualifying territory (s 931C; broadly a territory with a treaty containing a non-discrimination provision); not an interest-like distribution (CTA 2010 s 1000(1) E or F); no deduction allowed abroad; not a tax advantage scheme s 931B
Medium or large company Within an exempt class; not an E or F distribution; no deduction allowed abroad s 931D

The exempt classes (one is enough).

Class Detail Reference
Controlled companies Condition A: the recipient controls the payer. Condition B (joint venture): the recipient is one of two persons who together control the payer, holds ≥ 40%, and the other holds ≥ 40% but ≤ 55%. Control as in TIOPA 2010 s 371RB (read with s 371RD as modified) s 931E; INTM653030
Non-redeemable ordinary shares s 931F
Portfolio holdings Under 10% s 931G
Transactions not designed to reduce tax s 931H
Shares accounted for as liabilities s 931I
Anti-avoidance ss 931J–931Q (for example s 931J: schemes to bring pre-control profits within the controlled company class) INTM654020

Deductible dividends. If the payer gets a deduction abroad, the dividend is not exempt (s 931B(c)/s 931D(c)), and no underlying tax credit is given (TIOPA 2010 s 57(3)): only withholding tax is creditable.

Withholding tax on an exempt dividend is a pure cost. Tarnmoor Vallaria SA (TVS; 100% owned by TPLC) pays dividends exempt under the controlled company class; Vallaria withholds 15% under the invented treaty. For this example, suppose TVS pays £10m: Vallaria keeps £1.5m, which can never be credited because there is no UK tax.

The election to tax (s 931R). A company may elect for a distribution not to be exempt, within 2 years after the end of the AP of receipt. A typical reason (reasoned illustration): a source country grants its lower treaty withholding rate only if the dividend is taxable in the recipient’s hands, or credit would cover the UK tax anyway.

Worked example 25.4: does an election to tax help on Vallarian numbers? (labelled, not story)

A Vallarian subsidiary earns £900,000, pays Vallarian tax £180,000 and declares a dividend of £720,000, from which Vallaria withholds 15% (£108,000).

£
Dividend (gross of withholding) 720,000
Underlying tax (Step 2: £180,000; mixer cap (D + PA) × 25% = (720,000 + 180,000) × 25% = 225,000, not restrictive) 180,000
Taxable income (grossed up: s 31) 900,000
UK CT at 25% 225,000
Credit: underlying 180,000 + withholding 108,000 = 288,000, limited by s 42 (225,000)
UK tax nil
Foreign tax unrelieved 63,000

Total tax £288,000 either way: the election achieves nothing.

Exam lens: foreign dividends - Grade: core (“Company distributions received”, 1; chapter 19 owns domestic distributions). - Traps: treating a dividend as taxable with credit when it is exempt; forgetting that a dividend deductible abroad is neither exempt nor carries underlying tax relief; trying to credit withholding against nothing; applying the small-company test to a large group; confusing the s 42 limit with the s 58 mixer cap (chapter 24).

Branch or subsidiary.

In GY2, Tom Hesketh’s paper for Calder’s board ran the two routes side by side, on the same simplification that Vallaria taxes each period’s profit at 20%.

Worked example 25.5: Calder’s board paper, branch v subsidiary (invented)

£ Branch (no election) Vallarian subsidiary
Vallarian tax on £900,000 profit at 20% 180,000 180,000
UK relief for the £300,000 first-year loss (75,000) none: loss stays in Vallaria
UK top-up on £900,000 (25% − credit) 45,000 none: dividend exempt (s 931E)
Vallarian withholding on dividend of £720,000 at 15% — 108,000 (if fully distributed)
Total tax 150,000 288,000 (180,000 if retained)
CFC exposure n/a Tax exemption met: 20% ÷ 25% = 80% ≥ 75% (chapter 26)

For a short project that starts with a loss, the branch wins.

The general lesson is subtler. Over a long life, a profitable subsidiary in a lower-tax country keeps its lower rate, provided its profits are reinvested locally or come home without much withholding. A branch without an election is always topped up to the UK rate. The branch wins early, while losses need relief; the subsidiary, or an elected branch, wins later, when profits are steady.

Factor Branch (no election) Branch (elected) Subsidiary
Losses Relieved in the UK at once Not relieved in the UK Stay abroad
Rate on profits UK rate (credit tops up) Foreign rate only Foreign rate; dividends exempt
Foreign tax credit Yes (s 42 limits) No (s 18(3A)) Only if dividend taxed (s 931R)
Withholding on profits sent home None (same company) None On dividends: a pure cost
Anti-diversion — ss 18G–18I (CFC-shaped) CFC rules (TIOPA 2010 Part 9A)
Pricing PE attribution (CTA 2009 ss 20–21 for inbound; treaty Art 7) Same Transfer pricing (TIOPA 2010 Part 4)
Exit / change later Elect, or incorporate (s 140) Irrevocable Liquidate or sell (SSE: chapter 18)
Legal liability Company’s own Company’s own Ring-fenced
Residence risk — — Board must manage abroad (chapter 22)
Pillar Two Measured in the foreign jurisdiction in outline (chapter 30) Same Same
Scope Company-wide decision All PEs of the company Entity by entity

Exam lens: branch or subsidiary - M26 Q5 (20 marks) set exactly this choice. The examiners reported that many candidates wrongly discussed residence or migration of the UK company; the best answers covered PE thresholds, the branch exemption and its timing (losses), the impact of the overseas rate, and the subsidiary through CMC and CFC; some did TP although it was excluded; candidates also lost marks for “not mentioning obvious points (e.g. how CFC legislation works)”. - Layout: three options in turn; a short tax-cost comparison; a recommendation naming the option and the main reason.

Incorporating a branch.

TCGA 1992 s 140 (core within the PE/branch row; examined N25 Q2 and M23 Q2).

Condition Detail
Transferor UK resident company carrying on a trade outside the UK through a PE
Transfer The trade, with all its assets, or all except cash, to a non-UK resident company
Consideration Wholly or partly securities (shares, or shares and loan stock) in the transferee
Holding After the transfer, the transferor holds ≥ 25% of the transferee’s ordinary share capital
Claim The net gain is postponed in the proportion securities ÷ total consideration
Crystallisation (1) Transferor disposes of the securities (any time): postponed gain added to proceeds; (2) transferee disposes of the transferred assets within 6 years: the corresponding part of the postponed gain comes back

Worked example 25.6: s 140 postponement (labelled, not story)

£
Net gains on the branch’s assets 1,000,000
Consideration: shares 3,000,000 + cash 1,000,000 = 4,000,000
Postponed: 1,000,000 × 3,000,000 / 4,000,000 750,000
Chargeable now 250,000
CT at 25% 62,500

Judgement. (1) If the company has already elected under s 18A, gains on PE assets generally fall within the exempt amounts, so s 140 matters most for branches never exempt, or close companies (s 18P). (2) The new subsidiary is a foreign company controlled from the UK: CFC rules apply; plant transferred gives balancing adjustments; intangible fixed assets may give realisation credits (chapter 11). N25 Q2’s examiners noted that few candidates saw that the incorporation gain could be postponed.

ss 140A–140L (non-core). A family of reliefs born in EU law (F(No.2)A 1992 ss 45–49; SI 2007/3186 for mergers):

Section Relief (in outline)
s 140A (with s 140B anti-avoidance) Transfer of all or part of a UK business between companies resident in different relevant states, wholly for shares or debentures, assets remaining in the UK charge: no gain, no loss, on a joint claim. CAA 2001 s 561 follows through for capital allowances
s 140C (with s 140D) A UK company transfers a business carried on through a PE in a member State to a company resident in a member State, for securities: gains and losses netted; notional foreign tax credit under TIOPA 2010 s 122 where appropriate (CG45713)
ss 140E–140L Cross-border mergers (s 561A CAA 2001)

Since 31 December 2020, the Taxes (Amendments) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019 (SI 2019/689) reg 6 replaced “member State” with “relevant state” in s 140A, defined in s 140L(10) as the UK or a member State. The same regulation also amended s 140C (for example “another member State” became “a member State”, and “other than the United Kingdom” was omitted), so after Brexit s 140C still turns on a PE in, and a transferee resident in, an EU member State; treat its detailed post-Brexit scope with care. Vallaria is not a member State, so none of these reliefs helps Calder; Ireland is (chapter 31).

Exam lens: incorporation reliefs - Grades: s 140 within the core PE/branch row; “Transfers concerning companies of different member States” non-core (2). - N25 Q2: the marking guide gave marks for the “conditions for chargeable gain postponement”. State the conditions; compute the postponed proportion; mention crystallisation. - Trap: forgetting the 25% condition (a transfer to a sister company in which the transferor holds nothing fails).

Unremittable income.

Two separate reliefs; choosing the right one is the first mark.

Trading receipts Other foreign income
Statute CTA 2009 ss 173–175 (Part 3) CTA 2009 Part 18, ss 1274–1278
HMRC guidance BIM42750 CFC version: TIOPA 2010 s 371SN (INTM255820)
Test Amount brought into account as a trade receipt is unremittable because, and only because, of foreign exchange restrictions (local law, executive action, impossibility of obtaining transferable currency). HMRC: such a debt is not a bad or doubtful debt Condition A: income cannot be transferred to the UK because of local law, executive action of its government, or impossibility of obtaining transferable currency; Condition B: not realised outside the territory for sterling or a transferable currency (s 1274)
Relief Deduction from trading profits, not so as to create a loss; excess carried forward (s 173) On a claim, income not taken into account (s 1275); claim within 2 years after the end of the AP in which the income arises
Withdrawal Amount ceases to be unremittable, is exchanged for a remittable amount, is used to finance expenditure or investment outside the UK, an impairment is made, or (debts) insurance is received: treated as a trade receipt of that period (s 175) Relief withdrawn when the income ceases to be unremittable (s 1276); income charged after the source has ceased (s 1277); valuation (s 1278)

Worked example 25.7: TEL’s blocked receipt (labelled example; amounts for illustration)

In GY6 a Marrovian customer of Tarnmoor Engineering Ltd (TEL) pays £400,000 for pumps into a local bank account; new Marrovian exchange controls (Marrovia is invented) stop it leaving.

  • The sale is a receipt of TEL’s UK trade, so the relief is s 173, not a Part 18 claim.
  • GY6: £400,000 included in turnover; s 173 deduction (£400,000) (TEL’s trading profits are far larger, so no loss limit bites).
  • GY7: controls lift and the money is converted: relief withdrawn (s 175); £400,000 treated as a trading receipt of GY7.
  • Effect: £100,000 of CT deferred one year. Any exchange difference on conversion is a separate accounting and tax point.

Contrast: if the blocked amount were interest on a Marrovian deposit of a UK company with no trade there, Part 18 would apply, with a claim by the second anniversary of the end of the AP.

Exam lens: unremittable income - Grade: core (1). Not seen as a main topic M23–M26: expect a few marks inside an overseas question. - Traps: treating a blocked trade debt as a bad debt; using Part 18 for trading receipts; missing the 2-year Part 18 claim; forgetting that the relief defers, it does not exempt.

International movements of capital.

Until 2009, ICTA 1988 s 765 required prior Treasury consent for certain transactions moving capital outside the UK (for example, a UK company causing or permitting a foreign subsidiary to issue shares or debentures); s 765A required information for movements within Europe; s 766 made breach an offence. FA 2009 s 37 and Sch 17 repealed them and substituted reporting, for events and transactions on or after 1 July 2009.

Rule Detail Reference
UK corporate parent UK resident body corporate controlling one or more non-resident bodies corporate, not itself controlled by UK resident companies Sch 17 para 5
Reporting body Not foreign-controlled; or foreign-controlled with no other UK corporate parent; or nominated where a foreign parent has several Sch 17 paras 5–7
Reportable Value exceeding £100m and: issue of shares or debentures by a foreign subsidiary; transfer of shares or debentures of a foreign subsidiary by or caused by the reporting body; a foreign subsidiary becoming or ceasing to be a controlling partner; others prescribed Sch 17 para 8
Excluded Ordinary course of trade; all parties resident in the same territory; security given to a foreign subsidiary’s bankers; certain investment of funds; regulations Sch 17 para 9
Deadline Within 6 months of the event or transaction Sch 17 para 4
Penalty TMA 1970 s 98 (special returns) Sch 17 para 10

Worked example 25.8 (labelled hypothetical, not story). TVS issues £120m of new shares to TPLC to fund a new plant. TPLC is a UK corporate parent and, not being foreign-controlled, the reporting body. £120m > £100m; the parties are in different territories; an issue of shares by a foreign subsidiary is not in the ordinary course of trade. TPLC reports within 6 months.

Exam lens: international movements of capital - Grade: non-core (2). Expect 1–2 marks: who reports, the £100m threshold, 6 months, s 98 penalty.

Going further.

  • PE register. List every foreign PE, including construction sites and dependent agents that might create one (chapter 23): an election would capture all of them.
  • Model before each AP. The election can only start with the next AP. If made, schedule the opening negative amount and make any streaming election in the first relevant return.
  • One company, one answer. The election belongs to a company, not a group: loss-making ventures and mature branches can sit in different UK companies, one elected and one not. Some years later in our invented story, Tarnmoor buys Jess Hartley’s Ridgeway Holdings, whose subsidiary has a Dublin showroom branch with no election: chapter 31 decides it.
  • Repatriation. Dividends: usually exempt, but withholding is a cost. Interest, royalties and management charges: deductible abroad, taxable at home with credit for withholding, at arm’s length. TVS pays interest to TFL (£120m at 6%) and TCM, a royalty to Calder (from GY4; 5% withholding: chapter 24) and a management charge to TPLC; it can pay dividends (15% withholding).
  • Deadlines. s 931R election and Part 18 claims: 2 years after the AP end. IMC reports: 6 months. Streaming: first relevant return.
  • Record the reasoning. Minute a decision not to elect with the forecast behind it (as Calder did), so a later finance director knows why the company is where it is. Using elections Parliament offers, as intended, is ordinary tax management, not avoidance.
  • Watch the draft Bill. If enacted, the compulsory exemption would turn every branch decision into a question of transitional loss restriction for APs beginning on or after 1 January 2027.

How the examiner tests it.

The topic appears often, usually inside a larger international question: M23 Q2 (15), N25 Q2 (15), M26 Q5 (20) (details in the Exam lens boxes above). The favourite combination is PE + branch exemption + incorporation of the branch + CFC. The grades: branches and subsidiaries, foreign dividends and unremittable income core; cross-border transfer reliefs and international movements of capital non-core.

A good answer to a branch question sets out the three options in turn (taxable branch: credit relief and loss timing; elected branch: irrevocable, all PEs, opening negative amount; subsidiary: residence kept abroad, dividend exemption, withholding as a cost, CFC test), compares the tax cost over the periods given, and ends with a recommendation. Allow about 2.1 minutes a mark (about 42 minutes for 20 marks). Keep each table in £ or £000, not both.

What to take away.

  • A UK resident company is taxed on its profits wherever they arise (CTA 2009 s 5). Without an election, branch losses are relieved at once and branch profits are taxed at 25% with credit capped at UK tax on that income (TIOPA 2010 ss 42, 44): the branch’s net result is taxed at the UK rate.
  • s 18A election: removes profits and losses of every foreign PE, territory by territory, measured under the full treaty or the OECD Model (s 18S, updated to 18 November 2025); notional capital allowances. Applies from the relevant day (start of the next AP); revocable only before then; then irrevocable. No credit for foreign tax on exempt profits (s 18(3A)). Small companies: full treaty territories only; close companies’ gains excluded unless assets used solely for the PE (s 18P); investment business and UK land excluded; anti-diversion rule (ss 18G–18I) shaped like the CFC rules.
  • Opening negative amount (ss 18J–18N): 6-year look-back; net PE losses must be matched by later PE profits before exemption; streaming per territory in the first relevant return.
  • In our invented case, Calder’s Vallarian branch lost £300,000 (AP to 31 March GY3; UK relief £75,000), then made £900,000 (9-month AP to 31 December GY3): Vallarian tax £180,000, UK CT £225,000, top-up £45,000; project total £150,000 (25% of £600,000). Calder did not elect: by the time the profit was clear, an election could start only after the project ended. Hindsight: electing in the earlier AP would have saved £30,000 at the price of binding every future branch.
  • Subsidiary: own profits, losses and rate. Dividends exempt if in an exempt class (controlled companies incl. the 40/55 joint venture limb; non-redeemable ordinary shares; portfolio < 10%; transactions not designed to reduce tax; shares accounted as liabilities), unless deductible abroad (then no exemption and no underlying tax credit). Withholding on exempt dividends is a pure cost (TVS: 15%). s 931R election: within 2 years.
  • s 140: postponement on incorporating a foreign PE trade for securities, transferor ≥ 25%, in proportion securities ÷ consideration; crystallises on disposal of the securities, or of the assets within 6 years. ss 140A–140L: non-core; “relevant state” = UK or a member State.
  • Unremittable: trading receipts under ss 173–175 (no loss created; withdrawn when remittable or used abroad); other foreign income under Part 18 (claim within 2 years).
  • International movements of capital: reporting body; > £100m; within 6 months; TMA s 98.
  • Proposed, not law: a compulsory exemption for APs beginning on or after 1 January 2027 (draft of 13 July 2026).

So, branch or subsidiary? A branch while losses need relief; a subsidiary, or an elected branch, when profits are steady; and a recommendation either way. Under Finance Act 2026 it is still a choice.

Once a subsidiary exists, the UK still watches what it earns. Chapter 26, on controlled foreign companies, explains how.

Chapter twenty six: Controlled foreign companies.

A rule on trial.

On 19 September 2024 the Court of Justice of the European Union gave judgment in three joined appeals (Cases C-555/22 P, C-556/22 P and C-564/22 P). The appellants were the United Kingdom, the broadcaster ITV, and companies in the London Stock Exchange group. The defendant was the European Commission. The subject was a single exemption in the UK’s rules on controlled foreign companies: the exemption for group finance companies.

Five years earlier, on 2 April 2019 (Decision (EU) 2019/1352), the Commission had decided that part of that exemption was unlawful State aid. HMRC had been made to collect the money from the groups that had used it. The General Court had upheld the Commission on 8 June 2022 (Cases T-363/19 and T-456/19). Now the Court of Justice set that judgment aside and annulled the Commission’s decision. (The EU dates and case numbers come from the Court’s press release as reproduced by professional sources; the British steps that followed are in UK statute and are verified. We meet them later in the chapter.)

The legal error was a choice of baseline. To call a tax rule State aid, you must show that it departs from the normal rules. The Commission had treated the CFC rules themselves as the normal rules, and the finance company exemption as a departure from them. The Court of Justice held that the right reference framework was the UK’s corporation tax system as a whole. Look at the whole system, and a rule that chooses not to tax some foreign profits is not a gift: it is a decision about where the UK’s taxing reach should stop.

That is the question underneath this chapter. A UK company owns a subsidiary abroad. The subsidiary is a separate person, resident in another country, taxed there. Its profits are not the parent’s profits. When, if ever, should the UK tax them? And if it does, on whom, and how much?

This is chapter 26, in Part Four (profits that cross borders). Controlled foreign companies are core (grade 1) on the LCG Advanced Technical paper, and the examiners set full 20-mark CFC questions in May 2024 and May 2025. The Living Law (TKS), chapter 26, met the choice between a branch and a subsidiary abroad and the exemption for foreign dividends, and only signposted these rules. Chapter 25 of this book took the branch side of that choice; here we take the subsidiary side to Advanced Technical depth. Throughout, the law is that for FY2026, under Finance Act 2026.

The rules are in TIOPA 2010 Part 9A (ss 371AA–371VJ), “the International Act” in the audio edition. “CTA 2010” is the Corporation Tax Act 2010.

Why the rules exist.

Every growing group faces the choice. A UK company that sells abroad can do it through a branch or through a subsidiary. Chapter 25 showed that a branch is part of the UK company, so its profits are UK profits unless the company elects for the branch exemption (CTA 2009 s 18A). A subsidiary is its own taxpayer. If it is resident abroad, the UK taxes nothing it earns abroad; it taxes the parent only on what comes back, and since 1 July 2009 most dividends that come back are exempt (CTA 2009 Part 9A).

That is a sensible design for genuine foreign business. A factory in Vallaria (an invented country, home of our story’s main foreign subsidiary) should pay Vallarian tax on Vallarian profits. But the design opens a door. Suppose a UK group moves money, a valuable patent or a profitable contract into a subsidiary in a country with a very low tax rate, with few people and no reason to exist except the rate. Profits that used to arise in the UK now arise there. That is not a foreign business. It is UK profit wearing a foreign coat.

A controlled foreign company regime looks through the coat. Where a non-UK company is controlled from the UK and some of its profits look as though they belong in the UK, the regime taxes those profits on the UK companies that own it.

The old regime (1984 to 2012). The UK first introduced CFC rules in 1984 (later ICTA 1988 Part 17 Ch 4, ss 747–756). Broadly, the old regime cast a wide net over controlled companies taxed at a low level abroad and then released those that passed one of a set of exclusions. HMRC’s manual (INTM254220) lists them: the acceptable distribution policy (paying broadly 90% of net chargeable profits home as dividends within 18 months: INTM254610), the exempt activities test, the de minimis exclusion (£50,000, pro-rated), the excluded countries regulations, the motive test, and a territorial exclusion. The ADP exemption was abolished for periods beginning on or after 1 July 2009, when the dividend exemption arrived, because a dividend home no longer produced UK tax.

Europe. In Cadbury Schweppes plc v IRC (Case C-196/04), judgment of the Grand Chamber on 12 September 2006 on a reference from the Special Commissioners, the Court of Justice held that rules of this kind restrict freedom of establishment and can be justified only where they target “wholly artificial arrangements” intended to escape the national tax normally payable. A subsidiary actually established in another member state and carrying on genuine economic activities there could not be taxed this way, even if tax had been a reason for putting it there. The Court pointed to objective factors that third parties can verify, such as premises, staff and equipment.

The UK statute did not say that. In Vodafone 2 v HMRC, the High Court (Evans-Lombe J, [2008] EWHC 1569 (Ch), 4 July 2008) held that no conforming interpretation was possible, so the rules had to be disapplied for EU subsidiaries. The Court of Appeal reversed that on 22 May 2009 (Vodafone 2 v HMRC [2009] EWCA Civ 446; the Chancellor of the High Court, Longmore and Goldring LJJ): the legislation could be read as containing an additional exception for a CFC actually established in another member state and carrying on genuine economic activities there. Vodafone 2 Ltd’s Luxembourg subsidiary had held the Mannesmann shares bought in 2000 (secondary summaries of the judgment). The rules survived, but with a patch sewn on by the courts.

A regime that caught too much and then excused too much was ready for replacement.

The twenty twelve answer.

FA 2012 s 180 and Sch 20 inserted Part 9A into TIOPA 2010 and repealed the old rules. The new regime applies to CFC accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2013 (FA 2012 Sch 20 paras 49–50; a company already a CFC on that date began a new-regime AP then; a straddling old-regime period ran on to its end). Its starting idea is the reverse of the old one: instead of catching everything and excusing some, it aims to tax only profits artificially diverted from the UK, and it defines them by rule.

The defining device is the gateway. Picture a sieve over the UK tax base. A foreign subsidiary’s profits are poured in; most fall away, because they belong where they were earned; only profits that belong in the UK drop through. Beside the sieve are doors: a company that passes through a door walks past the sieve entirely.

The precise rule. Under s 371BA(2) a CFC charge arises for a CFC’s AP only if (a) the CFC has chargeable profits and (b) none of the entity exemptions (Chapters 10–14) applies. Chargeable profits are the CFC’s assumed taxable total profits (ATTP: profits computed as if the CFC were UK resident, under the “CT assumptions” in Ch 19, ss 371SB–371SR) so far as they pass through the gateway (s 371BA(3), s 371BB). The doors are the entity exemptions; the sieve is the gateway.

The five charging steps (s 371BC).

Step What happens Reference
1 Identify the relevant persons and their relevant interests; stop if none is a UK resident company Ch 15
2 Compute the CFC’s creditable tax Ch 16, s 371PA
3 Apportion chargeable profits and creditable tax Ch 17
4 Identify the chargeable companies (≥ 25% with connected and associated persons) s 371BD
5 Charge = appropriate rate × P% × chargeable profits − Q% × creditable tax, as CT of the chargeable company for its AP in which the CFC’s AP ends s 371BC(1), (3)–(4)

The appropriate rate is the main rate for the chargeable company’s AP (averaged if the AP straddles a change): 25% for FY2026.

Exam lens: the order of attack - Grade: controlled foreign companies 1 (core) (2026 grid; also 1 in the 2028 grid). - Layout the examiners reward: company by company: (1) is it a CFC (control)? (2) does an entity exemption apply? if so, stop; (3) which gateway chapters apply and what passes? (4) apportionment and the 25% test; (5) creditable tax and the charge. - Trap: candidates kept discussing other exemptions after finding one that applied (M24 Q5 examiners’ report, paraphrased).

The theory of the gateway. The regime borrows its central test from the OECD’s 2010 Report on the Attribution of Profits to Permanent Establishments (the AOA): where are the significant people functions (SPFs), the people who take the decisions about assets and risks? If they are in the UK, the profits they generate belong to the UK (s 371DA(3)). (The OECD report was not opened for this book; the statute’s reference to it was.)

Who is a controlled foreign company.

A CFC is a company that is not UK resident and is controlled by a UK resident person or persons (s 371AA(3)). The controllers need not be companies, although only companies are charged. The Part does not displace the ordinary charge on a non-resident company’s UK permanent establishment (s 371AA(11)).

Test Rule Reference
Legal control Power, through shares, votes or the articles, to secure that C’s affairs are conducted as P wishes s 371RB(1)
Economic control P would receive > 50% of the proceeds on a sale of all the share capital, or of income distributed, or of assets on a winding up (lending banks’ rights ignored) s 371RB(2)–(6)
Joint control Two or more persons together meeting either test s 371RB(7)
40% rule One UK and one non-UK controller: C is a CFC if the UK person holds ≥ 40% and the non-UK person holds ≥ 40% but ≤ 55% s 371RC
Attribution Future rights, nominees’ rights and (for UK persons) rights of connected UK persons s 371RD
Accounting control P is C’s parent under the relevant accounting standard, and the 50% condition: at least 50% of chargeable profits would be apportioned to P and its UK subsidiaries s 371RE
> 50% investment A UK resident company, alone or with associated enterprises (25% investment links), directly or indirectly has more than a 50% investment in C s 371RG (FA 2019 s 20(4)); CFC APs beginning on or after 1 January 2019

The 40% rule matters for joint ventures. Without it, it is not obvious that a company controlled jointly by a UK person and a foreign person is “controlled by UK resident persons”. The rule answers that: a 50:50 venture between a UK group and a French group is a CFC (UK 50% ≥ 40%; partner 50% ≤ 55%); a company run by a foreign partner with 60% is not.

The > 50% investment rule was the UK’s implementation of the EU Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive (ATAD) control test. It remains UK law after Brexit.

CFC residence and accounting periods. A CFC is resident in the territory where it is liable to tax by reason of domicile, residence or place of management, with tie-breakers where there is more than one (ss 371TA–371TC). A CFC’s AP begins when it becomes a CFC and ends on events such as ceasing to be one, becoming or ceasing to be liable to tax in a territory, or a relevant interest holder ceasing to have any interest; otherwise CTA 2009 s 10 applies (s 371VB). The charge falls in the chargeable company’s AP in which the CFC’s AP ends.

Doors past the sieve.

The five entity exemptions are in Chapters 10–14. If any applies for an AP, there is no charge for that AP: no gateway, no apportionment. Test them in order and stop at the first that works.

The exempt period (Ch 10, ss 371JA–371JG)

When a company first comes under UK control (typically on acquisition), the group gets 12 months of grace to restructure. HMRC (INTM224200) summarises the starting conditions: the company exists, is resident outside the UK, is controlled from the UK and has at least one chargeable company, and for the preceding 12 months it had no chargeable companies and the charging condition was not met. A CFC AP that ends in the exempt period is exempt (INTM224175) if:

  • the subsequent period condition (s 371JB(2)) is met: the company must not cease to be a CFC before an AP beginning after the exempt period, and the CFC charge must not apply to that following AP. The grace is for groups that use the year to put things right; and
  • the chargeable company condition (s 371JB(3)): only original chargeable companies, or companies connected with them, benefit.

Profits of a straddling AP that arise in the exempt period are removed (s 371JE). Anti-avoidance applies to finance and IP arrangements and artificially short APs (s 371JF). Because whether the subsequent period condition is met is known only later, a return may be amended up to 12 months after the filing date for the AP in which the first post-exempt-period CFC AP ends (s 371JG). HMRC may extend the exempt period by notice given before it ends.

Worked example 26.1: exempt period (labelled hypothetical, not story) Suppose our invented group, Tarnmoor (introduced below), bought a Marrovian distributor on 1 March, year end 31 December. Exempt period: 1 March to the end of the following February. First CFC AP: 1 March–31 December, ending inside the exempt period: exempt, provided the subsequent period condition is met. Next AP (1 January–31 December) straddles the end of the exempt period: only profits arising after the exempt period are in the frame (s 371JE).

Excluded territories (Ch 11, ss 371KA–371KJ)

A CFC resident in a territory listed in the Controlled Foreign Companies (Excluded Territories) Regulations 2012 (SI 2012/3024, Schedule Part 1; in force 1 January 2013) is exempt if its categories A–D income (broadly, income benefiting from exemptions, incentives, refunds or notional interest) does not exceed a threshold: the greater of 10% of accounting profits and £50,000 (pro-rated for short APs), plus an IP condition and no main-purpose tax arrangement. For Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Japan and the USA, HMRC’s manual says the income and IP conditions need not be met if residence and no-foreign-PE requirements are met (INTM225100, page dated 2016; the regulations themselves were not opened for this book: check them).

Low profits (Ch 12, ss 371LA–371LC)

Exempt if accounting profits or ATTP are ≤ £50,000; or ≤ £500,000 with non-trading income ≤ £50,000. All figures are pro-rated for APs under 12 months. Anti-avoidance: arrangements to fall within it; UK intermediary services businesses; the £50,000 limbs are unavailable where the group mismatch scheme rules (CTA 2010 Part 21B) bite.

Worked example 26.2: thresholds in short periods (labelled)

£
Low profits, 9-month AP: £500,000 × 9/12 375,000
Non-trading income limit, 9-month AP: £50,000 × 9/12 37,500
Excluded territories threshold, accounting profits £300,000: greater of £30,000 and £50,000 50,000
Excluded territories threshold, accounting profits £2,000,000: greater of £200,000 and £50,000 200,000

The low profit margin and the tax exemption.

Low profit margin (Ch 13, ss 371MA–371MC)

For routine, low-margin activity (a distributor, a service centre). A CFC is exempt if its accounting profits are no more than 10% of its relevant operating expenditure (ROE). Two details decide almost every answer:

  1. Profits are measured before any deduction for interest (s 371MB(2)): interest expense is added back, but interest income stays in (INTM225800). A finance company cannot use the rule to strip out its own interest income.
  2. ROE is operating expenditure in the accounts excluding (a) the cost of goods purchased that are not used in the CFC’s territory, and (b) expenditure that gives rise to income of a related person (s 371MB). A management fee to the UK parent is the classic (b) item. s 371MC adds anti-avoidance: no exemption where arrangements have a main purpose of securing it.

“Accounting profits” are pre-tax profits under an acceptable GAAP, ignoring exempt distributions, property business profits or losses and capital profits; Part 4 transfer pricing applies, but a difference of £50,000 or less is ignored (ss 371VC–371VD).

Worked example 26.3: low profit margin (labelled; the M25 trap)

£
Sales 6,000,000
Cost of goods (of which 1,500,000 shipped direct to customers outside the CFC’s territory) (4,200,000)
Staff (700,000)
Management fee to UK parent (300,000)
Rent (200,000)
Other (150,000)
Operating expenditure (5,550,000)
Profit before interest 450,000
Interest (90,000)
Profit after interest 360,000
Relevant operating expenditure £
Operating expenditure 5,550,000
Less goods not used in the territory (1,500,000)
Less expenditure giving rise to a related person’s income (fee) (300,000)
ROE 3,750,000
10% of ROE 375,000

£450,000 > £375,000: the exemption fails. Wrong method: £360,000 (after interest) against £555,000 (10% of total opex) gives a false “exempt”. Next: test the tax exemption, then the gateway.

The tax exemption (Ch 14, ss 371NA–371NE)

A CFC is exempt if its local tax amount is at least 75% of the corresponding UK tax. The corresponding UK tax is CT on the CFC’s ATTP under the CT assumptions, ignoring DTR for the local tax and less any UK income tax or CT actually suffered on that income. At 25%, the break-even local rate on an identical base is 75% × 25% = 18.75%.

Both sides are adjusted. Local tax is tax paid in the CFC’s territory on its local chargeable profits (excluding capital gains), reduced where the local base includes income not in ATTP, where ATTP deducts expenses the local system does not, and by repayments or credits to any person (s 371NC). Tax under designer rate provisions does not count (s 371ND). A company on a tax holiday has a local tax amount of nil and never passes.

Worked example 26.4: tax exemption with an adjustment (labelled)

£
ATTP 1,200,000
Corresponding UK tax at 25% 300,000
75% hurdle 225,000
Local tax: 18% × local profits 1,300,000 234,000
Less 18% × 100,000 of local income not in ATTP (18,000)
Local tax amount 216,000 (72%)

Not exempt. The unadjusted comparison (234,000 / 300,000 = 78%) would wrongly exempt it.

The five doors share a logic: each is Parliament’s advance judgement that a whole company is unlikely to be a vehicle for diverted UK profit: a new acquisition, a company in a respectable system, a small company, a low-margin company, a company paying proper tax at home.

Exam lens: the entity exemptions - Grade: core (within CFCs). - Past appearances: M24 Q5 (20 marks: five overseas companies; tax rate comparisons; a tax-holiday company): exemptions good on the whole. M25 Q1 (20 marks): few calculated the low profit margin correctly; the exempt period was well understood. - Traps: profit before interest; trim ROE for goods not used locally and related-person expenditure; adjust both sides of the tax exemption; tax holidays and designer rates fail; pro-rate thresholds for short APs; stop at the first exemption that works.

Which gateway chapters apply.

The gateway has two stages (s 371BB). Chapter 3 decides which of Chapters 4–8 apply; each applicable chapter then decides how much passes. If none applies, nothing passes: no chargeable profits.

Chapter 4: profits attributable to UK activities

Ch 4 applies unless any one of Conditions A–D is met (s 371CA):

Condition Met if…
A The CFC holds no assets and bears no risks under arrangements a main purpose of which is to reduce UK tax and which are expected to make it more profitable (and would not have been made but for the expected tax reduction)
B The CFC holds no UK-managed assets or risks
C The CFC itself has the capability to ensure its business would be commercially effective if UK management stopped
D Its assumed total profits consist only of non-trading finance profits and/or property business profits

A genuine foreign trading company run by local management usually escapes Ch 4 through A or B.

The eight steps (s 371DB) where Ch 4 applies:

  1. Identify the CFC’s assets and risks.
  2. Exclude negligible ones.
  3. Identify the SPFs relevant to them, treating the CFC group as one company.
  4. Split UK and non-UK SPFs; stop if there are no UK SPFs.
  5. Hypothesise a UK PE carrying on the UK SPFs; attribute to it the assets and risks they manage.
  6. Exclude assets and risks where UK activity is the minority (s 371DC: amount A ≤ 50% of amount B).
  7. Recompute the CFC’s profits without the PE-attributed assets and risks (“provisional Chapter 4 profits”); the difference passes…
  8. …subject to the exclusions in ss 371DD–371DF.

The exclusions: economic value (arrangements create substantial non-tax value: s 371DD); independent companies (independent parties would have made the same arrangements on the same terms: s 371DE); and the trading profits safe harbour (s 371DF), all five conditions:

Condition Test Reference
Business premises Premises in its territory with a reasonable degree of permanence; activities wholly or mainly from there (building sites only if ≥ 12 months) s 371DG
Income ≤ 20% of relevant trading income from UK residents or UK PEs (banks ≤ 10%) s 371DH
Management expenditure UK-related management expenditure ≤ 20% of total (or the 50% per-asset alternative) s 371DI
IP No significant IP transferred from UK related persons in the AP or the previous 6 years s 371DJ
Export of goods ≤ 20% of trading income from goods exported from the UK (other than to the CFC’s territory) s 371DK

Anti-avoidance stops reorganisations designed to meet the tests (s 371DL). The safe harbour turns on facts a group can see and manage, so that a well-run foreign trading company need not commission a people-functions study every year.

Finance profits.

Money is the easiest thing to move, so it has its own chapters.

Chapter 5: non-trading finance profits (NTFP)

Ch 5 applies where the CFC has NTFP (s 371CB), but NTFP from funds held for the purposes of the CFC’s own trade or property business are left out, unless the funds are held for something else (future dividends, acquisitions, contingencies, or a tax-reduction purpose).

The 5% incidental rule (s 371CC): if the CFC has trading or property profits, Ch 5 does not apply where its NTFP are ≤ 5% of its trading and property profits (before interest and tax). A similar rule protects mainly-holding companies with exempt distribution income (s 371CD).

Worked example 26.5: the 5% rule (labelled) Trading profits before interest and tax £3,000,000; NTFP £140,000. 5% = £150,000. £140,000 ≤ £150,000: Ch 5 does not apply.

What passes where Ch 5 applies (ss 371EA–371EE):

Route Catches Reference
UK activities NTFP attributable to UK SPFs (the Ch 4 test applied to finance profits) s 371EB
Capital investment from the UK NTFP earned on funds derived from capital contributions by UK connected companies, from profits already charged as CFC profits, from s 174 claims, or other funds received from UK connected companies otherwise than for goods or services or by loan (with a deduction for undercharged management costs) s 371EC
Arrangements in lieu of dividends Arrangements made instead of paying dividends to UK companies, with a tax main reason s 371ED
Finance leases Finance leases to UK connected companies in lieu of purchase s 371EE

Put plainly: if a UK parent puts equity into a foreign finance company and the finance company lends it on, the interest is caught by s 371EC.

Chapters 6–8

  • Ch 6, trading finance profits (s 371CE, s 371FA): pass only so far as they arise from excess free capital (more than a non-51%-subsidiary would hold) derived from UK connected capital contributions. A group treasury company may elect, by notice within 20 months after the AP, to treat trading finance profits as NTFP (so that Ch 9 can apply).
  • Ch 7, captive insurance (s 371CF, s 371GA): insurance of UK connected risks.
  • Ch 8, solo consolidation (s 371CG, s 371HA): bank capital structures. Recognise; rarely examined.

The finance company exemptions.

Chapter 9 (ss 371IA–371IJ) is where the State aid saga began, and where Tarnmoor’s CFC lives.

Entry conditions (s 371IA): Ch 5 applies; the NTFP include profits of qualifying loan relationships (QLRs); and the CFC meets the business premises condition (s 371DG). A chargeable company may then claim (in its CT return; s 371IJ).

QLR (ss 371IG–371IH): a creditor relationship whose ultimate debtor is a qualifying company (connected with the CFC and controlled by the same UK persons). It is not a QLR if the debtor’s debits reduce the profits of a UK PE or a UK property business, if the debtor is a UK company without a s 18A election, or if they reduce another CFC’s chargeable profits.

QLR profits (s 371IA(4)) are QLR profits within s 371EC and not within s 371EB: since FA 2019 s 20(2), for CFC APs beginning on or after 1 January 2019, profits from UK SPFs cannot be exempted.

Exemption Rule Effect at 25% Reference
Full exemption X% exempt if X% of the principal is funded wholly out of qualifying resources (e.g. profits from lending to group companies in the debtor’s territory used there; funds from shares in group members derived from local business profits, pre-acquisition funds or external non-redeemable ordinary share issues); debtor resident in one territory Nil ss 371IB, 371IC
75% exemption Where the full exemption is not claimed for a QLR: 75% of its profits exempt 25% passes: 25% × 25% = 6.25% before credit s 371ID
Matched interest Remaining QLR profits (“matched interest profits”) exempt so far as the UK share exceeds the worldwide group’s aggregate net tax-interest expense (CIR, TIOPA Part 10) Nil if ANTIE is nil; nothing if ANTIE is large s 371IE

The current s 371IE (substituted by F(No.2)A 2017 for worldwide group periods of account beginning on or after 1 April 2017): if ANTIE is nil, matched interest profits are fully exempt (s 371IE(3)); otherwise, where the relevant proportion (each relevant chargeable company’s step 5 percentage × matched interest profits, summed: s 371IE(5)) exceeds ANTIE, the excess is exempt (s 371IE(4)). HMRC’s example (INTM219380): matched interest profits 25, ANTIE 9: 16 exempt. ANTIE for this purpose ignores banking and insurance amounts (s 371IE(8)). (Statute and INTM219380 seen in search extracts; the older INTM219250 formula predates 2017 and should not be used.)

Going further: designing a finance company that works - Premises and people first. Ch 9 needs the business premises condition, and since FA 2019 only profits outside s 371EB qualify. A finance company whose credit decisions are taken in the UK has UK SPFs: those profits pass through s 371EB and cannot be exempted. Local directors with real authority, local staff who assess and monitor the loans, and minutes that show it are the substance. - Choose the borrowers. Loans to foreign group companies controlled by the same UK persons qualify; loans to UK companies (without a s 18A election), to borrowers whose interest reduces UK PE or UK property profits, or to other CFCs whose chargeable profits it would reduce, do not. - Funding. Equity from the UK puts the profits inside s 371EC (that is why Ch 9 is needed at all). Funding from qualifying resources (local profits of the debtor’s territory, pre-acquisition funds, external ordinary share issues) can unlock the full exemption: track the source of funds loan by loan. - Matched interest. Only useful to groups whose UK net interest expense is small; check ANTIE each year (chapter 28). - The price of a claim. The 25% that passes still raises the parent’s s 105(3A) threshold; model that with the group relief plan. - Trading groups. For a foreign trading subsidiary, aim for Ch 3 Condition A or B (no tax-motivated arrangements; no UK-managed assets or risks), and keep the safe harbour’s five facts (premises, UK income, UK management expenditure, UK IP, UK exports) inside the limits.

Exam lens: gateways and Chapter 9 - Grade: core. - Past appearances: N23 Q1(c): a finance company paying 1% tax taken through the NTFP gateway (good answers; some strayed into DPT and CIR). M24 Q5: gateways answered less well than exemptions. - What earns marks: Ch 3 Conditions A–D and why Ch 4 is or is not switched off; the 5% rule; s 371EC (UK equity); the Ch 9 claim with the business premises condition; 75% exemption arithmetic (6.25%); QLR exclusions (UK debtor; UK PE).

From chargeable profits to the charge.

Chargeable profits are not yet tax. Two thresholds must be kept apart: control decides whether the foreign company is a CFC; the 25% test decides which UK companies pay. The examiners reported after M24 that candidates confused the 25% apportionment threshold with the control tests.

Relevant interests (s 371OC). A UK resident company’s interest is relevant except an indirect interest held through another UK resident company: the charge sits at the lowest UK company in the chain.

Apportionment (ss 371QC–371QG). Where all relevant persons hold only ordinary shares of one class (and other conditions hold), apportion by P% of the ordinary shares; indirect holdings multiply through the chain (s 371QE); holdings that vary are time-weighted (s 371QF). Otherwise, just and reasonable; HMRC may substitute its own basis (s 371UC); anti-avoidance apportionment (s 371QG).

Worked example 26.6: chains and time-weighting (labelled) - Indirect: UK plc holds 80% of X (non-UK), which holds 70% of the CFC: P% = 80% × 70% = 56%. - Time-weighted: 60% for 146 days then 100% for 219 days (365-day AP): P% = 60% × 146/365 + 100% × 219/365 = 84%.

Chargeable companies (s 371BD). A UK resident company is chargeable only if the percentage apportioned to it plus the percentages apportioned to persons connected or associated with it is at least 25%. (Exclusions for certain offshore fund managers and participants: ss 371BE–371BG.)

Creditable tax (s 371PA) is the sum of: (a) the DTR that would be given to the CFC (on the assumptions) for foreign tax on income included in its chargeable profits; (b) UK income tax deducted at source on that income (CTA 2010 s 967); (c) UK income tax or CT actually charged on it; (d) other countries’ CFC charges. Amounts repaid are excluded. It is apportioned like the profits.

Worked example 26.7: apportionment and the 25% test (labelled) FinCo (territory rate 5%) lends to a fellow subsidiary; interest £2,000,000; funded by UK equity; business premises; no UK SPFs; no entity exemption (5% local tax is 20% of UK tax). Shareholders: UK plc 80%, an unconnected UK company 15%, a non-UK investor 5%.

£
NTFP through s 371EC 2,000,000
75% exemption (s 371ID) (1,500,000)
Chargeable profits 500,000
Creditable tax: 5% × 500,000 (just and reasonable attribution assumed) 25,000
Holder % 25% test Charge £
UK plc 80 80% ≥ 25%: chargeable 25% × 80% × 500,000 − 80% × 25,000 = 100,000 − 20,000 = 80,000
Unconnected UK company 15 15% with no connected holders: not chargeable nil
Non-UK investor 5 outside the charge nil

Without the Ch 9 claim: 25% × 80% × 2,000,000 − 80% × 100,000 = £320,000. Variant: if the 15% holder were connected with UK plc, its own 15% plus UK plc’s 80% would pass the 25% test, and it too would be chargeable on its 15%.

Three consequences. 1. No reliefs against the charge. s 371UD (relief against the sum charged) was omitted by F(No.2)A 2015 s 36 for CFC APs beginning on or after 8 July 2015. Losses, management expenses and group relief cannot reduce it. 2. The profit-related threshold. CFC chargeable profits apportioned to a company under step 3 (where it is a chargeable company at step 4) are added to its profit-related threshold for surrendering management expenses and other s 99(1)(d)–(g) amounts as group relief (CTA 2010 s 105(3A)): chapter 13. 3. It is corporation tax of the chargeable company: returns, enquiries, assessments, interest and penalties all apply (s 371UA).

The misconception: “every low-taxed foreign subsidiary is caught”. People believe it because the old regime was built that way and because low tax is what the rules are about. But the modern regime asks three questions before anyone pays: does an entity exemption apply; do any profits pass the gateway; does a UK company hold at least 25%? A low-taxed subsidiary that trades with real local management, earns a low margin, or is simply small pays nothing. A highly taxed one never gets past the tax exemption.

Tarnmoor’s annual review.

Now our invented group. Tarnmoor plc (TPLC) is a widely held, London-listed engineering group; everything about it, its companies, its people and the countries Vallaria and Marrovia, is invented for teaching. Every year its head of tax, Tom Hesketh, runs a CFC review of each overseas subsidiary before the group’s return is prepared. We join the review for GY5, running the numbers on FY2026 rules.

Tarnmoor Capital Ltd (TCM)

Marrovian finance company; Marrovian CT 9% (invented; no UK treaty). Funded entirely by TPLC equity: £60m pre-story and £30m on 1 January GY5. Office and staff in Marrovia; its board meets there and its own team makes the lending decisions (no UK SPFs). Lends £60m to TVS and, from 1 January GY5, £30m to TIL (Irish resident since its migration on 30 June GY4), both at 6%.

Tarnmoor Vallaria SA (TVS)

Manufacturing and distribution subsidiary. Vallarian CT 20% on a base Tom’s team has reconciled to the UK computation: 20/25 = 80% of the corresponding UK tax ≥ 75%. Tax exemption applies: stop. (Its earlier UK PE question, chapter 23, is a matter of the non-resident charge, which Part 9A does not displace: s 371AA(11).)

Tarnmoor Ireland Ltd (TIL)

Irish-incorporated; UK resident by central management and control until it migrated on 30 June GY4 (chapter 22); a CFC from then (TPLC 100%).
