Chapter thirty: The global minimum and the end of diverted profits tax.

A floor under the world.

In October 2021, more than 135 countries agreed something that tax policy had never managed before. They agreed a minimum. The largest multinational groups would pay at least 15% on their profits in every country where they operate, or someone, somewhere, would collect the difference. The deal was struck through the OECD and its wider Inclusive Framework. The UK wrote its share of the deal into the Finance (No. 2) Act 2023, Parts 3 and 4 (“the Pillar Two legislation”).

Seven years earlier, the UK had reached for a blunter weapon. In his Autumn Statement on 3 December 2014, the Chancellor, George Osborne, announced a diverted profits tax (DPT). The press called it the “Google tax”. It sat outside corporation tax, charged a higher rate than corporation tax, and made the company pay before it could argue. For accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026, it is gone. Its work now belongs to a charge inside corporation tax, on what the law calls unassessed transfer pricing profits (UTPP).

Both changes share a single idea: profit should be taxed somewhere, at a fair rate, and a group that shifts it away should gain nothing. So this chapter asks two linked questions. When a large group’s profits end up somewhere taxed below the floor, who collects the difference? And now that DPT has gone, what stops a group from pricing its own dealings so that profit quietly leaves the UK?

This is chapter 30, the last chapter of Part Four (profits that cross borders). Everything in it is awareness (grade 3) on the LCG Advanced Technical paper: multinational top-up tax, domestic top-up tax and diverted profits tax. None was examined between May 2023 and May 2026. The Living Law (TKS) only signposted these rules, so we start from first principles, but keep to the depth an awareness topic deserves. Its close neighbours are chapters 26 (CFCs) and 27 (transfer pricing). Throughout, the law is that for FY2026, under Finance Act 2026.

Why a minimum tax.

Start with the problem. Profit is easy to move and hard to pin down. A group can put its patents, brands or lending in a subsidiary in a low-tax country and pay that subsidiary royalties or interest from everywhere else. Transfer pricing asks whether the price is right (chapter 27). CFC rules ask whether the parent’s country should tax the subsidiary’s profit (chapter 26). But neither touches the low rate itself, and for decades countries competed on that rate, each cutting a little to attract the mobile profit of large groups.

The minimum tax does not forbid a low rate. A country may still tax at 9%, or at nothing. What changes is that the low rate stops working for the largest groups, because the difference up to 15% is collected anyway. Picture a floor fitted under every country’s tax rate: if a country leaves a gap below the floor, another country fills it. The precise rule: for each country (territory) where a group operates, the group works out an effective tax rate on a common measure of profit; where that rate is below 15%, a top-up tax brings it up to 15%.

In December 2021 the OECD published model rules, the Global Anti-Base Erosion (GloBE) rules. As commentators describe the arrangement, countries were not obliged to adopt them, but those that did were expected to follow the model so that the pieces would fit together across borders. A floor only works if every country measures the room the same way. The whole project is usually called Pillar Two. (A separate “Pillar One” is not on this paper.)

The debate (L5). Is it a good idea? The paper will not ask you to settle it. Supporters say it ends a race to the bottom that drained public revenue and rewarded paper structures over real investment. Critics say it erodes a country’s right to set its own taxes, blunts the incentives small economies use to attract real activity, and buries large groups in compliance. Both points have force, and economists still argue about the evidence. The law, for now, has chosen the floor, and the UK has built it into two taxes.

The United Kingdom’s two taxes, and who is in.

Multinational top-up tax (MTT) Domestic top-up tax (DTT)
Where F(No.2)A 2023 Part 3 (ss 121–264) F(No.2)A 2023 Part 4 (s 265 ff)
From APs commencing on or after 31 December 2023 (s 264) APs commencing on or after 31 December 2023
Who pays UK parent members of qualifying groups, on low-taxed members abroad (income inclusion rule); from 31 December 2024 also the undertaxed profits rule (Part 3 Ch 9A, ss 229A–229J, inserted by FA 2025 Sch 4) UK entities of qualifying groups (and of large UK-only groups), on low-taxed UK profits
Nature IIR = main collection mechanism; UTPR = backstop (HMRC, MTT01100) The UK’s qualified domestic minimum top-up tax (QDMTT) (HMRC, MTT01200)

The income inclusion rule (IIR) makes a parent pay top-up tax on the low-taxed profits of its members abroad. The undertaxed profits rule (UTPR) is the backstop: where low-taxed profit escapes every IIR, perhaps because the parent’s country has none, other countries collect a share. Domestic top-up tax applies the same arithmetic to the group’s UK entities, so that any top-up on UK profit is collected by the UK, not by a parent’s country abroad.

So the order of collection is: (1) the country where the profit arises, through its own QDMTT, which HMRC’s guidance says is credited against GloBE top-up tax in the group calculation (with any shortfall still payable under the GloBE rules); (2) the parent’s country, through the IIR; (3) the UTPR, which mops up anything left.

Who is in (F(No.2)A 2023 s 129). A group is “qualifying” if the revenue in the ultimate parent entity’s consolidated financial statements exceeds €750m in at least two of the four previous accounting periods (periods other than 12 months scaled by days/365) (Condition A), and at least one member is located in the UK (Condition B). Notice “exceeds”: the statute says it, and so does HMRC’s manual (MTT01100). HMRC’s online guidance “Check if you need to report Pillar 2 top-up taxes” says “750 million euros or more”. The difference matters only for a group at exactly €750m; there, the statute governs.

Worked example 30.1: Tarnmoor in scope (invented)

Every company, person and country in the Tarnmoor group is invented for teaching. Tarnmoor plc (TPLC), widely held and listed in London, is the ultimate parent entity (UPE): the entity at the top of the consolidated accounts.

£m / €m GY1 GY2 GY3 GY4 GY5 GY6 GY7
Consolidated revenue (£m) 1,180 1,260 1,290 1,320 1,240 1,210 1,150
At the assumed €1.15 per £ (€m) 1,357 1,449 1,484 1,518 1,426 1,392 1,322
Exceeds €750m? Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes

The €1.15 rate is invented for illustration only (at that rate €750m is about £652m). For GY5 the test looks at GY1–GY4: all four exceed €750m, so two of four is met many times over. In our invented case Tarnmoor’s revenue exceeded €750m before GY1 (chapter 1), so TPLC registered long ago as the group’s filing member.

Measuring the rate.

The GloBE rules do not use any country’s own tax computation. They start from the accounting profit of each group entity, as used for the consolidated accounts, and make a set of adjustments of their own: the result is GloBE income. Against it they set covered taxes: broadly taxes on income, including the rules’ own deferred tax adjustments and some taxes paid by other members on that entity’s profit (such as a parent’s CFC charge: next section).

The effective tax rate (GloBE ETR) is worked out territory by territory, not company by company. All the group’s entities in one territory are blended:

Jurisdictional ETR = total covered taxes of the territory ÷ total GloBE income of the territory

If the ETR is below 15%, top-up percentage = 15% − ETR (HMRC, MTT01100).

The top-up percentage is not applied to the whole profit. First the rules deduct the substance-based income exclusion (SBIE): a deduction in proportion to the payroll costs and tangible assets the group has in the territory, which HMRC’s manual describes as corresponding to the return the group might expect on those assets and employees (MTT32000 ff). What remains is the excess profit, and the top-up percentage applies to that. A territory with many staff and factories may owe little or nothing even at a low rate; a territory holding only patents or loans gets almost no exclusion. (The SBIE percentages are not taught here; they are in the legislation and MTT32000–32030.) In the Tarnmoor figures below, we leave the SBIE out, which overstates the top-up a little, and treat accounting profit as GloBE income.

Misconception: “Under Pillar Two every company must pay at least 15%.” People believe it because the headline is “a 15% global minimum”. It is wrong in three ways: 1. It reaches only groups over the €750m threshold. 2. The test is a blended rate for each territory: one company at 10% and its sister at 20% may together clear the floor. 3. The measure is GloBE income and covered taxes, not taxable profit and tax paid. A UK company whose current tax is low because of full expensing does not by that alone create a top-up, because the GloBE rules count deferred tax as well.

As chapter 6 explained, the accounts themselves keep Pillar Two out of deferred tax under the temporary exception in IAS 12 para 4A (IASB, 23 May 2023), and show any Pillar Two current tax separately (para 88B).

So the rule is a floor for each territory of a large group, measured on its own base. It is not a minimum rate for each company.

Tarnmoor’s Marrovian test.

In our invented case, the group’s finance company, Tarnmoor Capital Ltd (TCM), is resident in Marrovia, an invented country with a corporation tax rate of 9% and, in the story, no domestic minimum tax of its own. In GY5 its profit is £5.1m (interest £5.4m less expenses £0.3m). Marrovian tax at 9% is £459,000.

The UK also taxes some of that profit. TCM is a CFC (chapter 26). After the finance company (Chapter 9) exemption, 25% of its profit is chargeable: £1,275,000. TPLC pays a CFC charge of £204,000 (25% × £1,275,000 = £318,750, less creditable Marrovian tax 9% × £1,275,000 = £114,750).

The Pillar Two step: F(No.2)A 2023 s 179 allocates a parent’s tax under a CFC tax regime (the UK CFC charge included) down to the CFC for MTT purposes, so it counts as a covered tax of Marrovia. For mobile income the amount pushed down is capped at (15% − local ETR) × that income. Here: 6% × £5.1m = £306,000. The CFC charge of £204,000 is within the cap, so all of it moves.

Worked example 30.2: Marrovia, GY5 (invented; simplified: SBIE ignored; accounting profit = GloBE income; no other GloBE adjustments)

£
GloBE income (TCM: interest 5,400,000 − expenses 300,000) 5,100,000
Covered taxes: Marrovian tax at 9% 459,000
Covered taxes: UK CFC charge pushed down (s 179) 204,000
Cap on push-down for mobile income: (15% − 9%) × 5,100,000 = 306,000; 204,000 within it
Total covered taxes 663,000
ETR (663,000 ÷ 5,100,000) 13.0%
Top-up percentage (15% − 13%) 2.0%
Excess profit (no SBIE in this simplification) 5,100,000
Top-up tax (2% × 5,100,000) 102,000
Less QDMTT paid in Marrovia (none: invented) —
MTT payable by TPLC under the IIR (inclusion ratio 100%) 102,000

Check: Marrovian tax £459,000 + CFC charge £204,000 + top-up £102,000 = £765,000 = 15.0% × £5.1m. Without the push-down, the ETR would be 9% and the top-up 6% × £5.1m = £306,000, the same total that the CFC charge and the top-up make together. The floor holds whichever route the money takes.

Why the ETR is always 13% here. The CFC charge is 25% × (25% − 9%) × profit = 4% of profit, so ETR = 9% + 4% = 13%, whatever the profit. In GY1–GY4 (TCM profit £3.3m; CFC charge £132,000; cap £198,000) the same arithmetic gives ETR 13.0% and a top-up of £66,000 a year (chapter 6’s GY2 rate reconciliation leaves it out as a simplification).

Elsewhere the floor does not bite on the story’s figures. - Vallaria taxes Tarnmoor Vallaria SA (TVS) at 20%: above 15%, no top-up (and, where available, the transitional safe harbour avoids the computation: below). - The UK companies pay 25%: on the story’s figures, no DTT. - Tarnmoor Ireland Ltd (TIL), Irish resident from 30 June GY4, pays Ireland’s 12.5% trading rate, below the floor. Who collects any Irish top-up depends on Irish law, which this paper does not examine (and this book has not researched); the story leaves it aside.

Safe harbours.

A full GloBE computation for every territory every year is a heavy task. Safe harbours treat a territory’s top-up as nil without the full calculation.

Transitional CbCR safe harbour (F(No.2)A 2023 Sch 16 Part 2, paras 3, 7–9). It borrows figures from the group’s (qualifying) country-by-country report. A group may elect for it for APs commencing on or before 31 December 2026 and ending on or before 30 June 2028. A territory passes if it meets any one of three tests:

Test Condition
De minimis Revenue < €10m and profit before tax < €1m
Simplified ETR Simplified covered taxes ÷ profit before tax ≥ 15% (periods beginning before 2025), 16% (beginning in 2025), 17% (beginning on or after 1 January 2026)
Routine profits Profit before tax ≤ the SBIE

And there is a sting: “once out, always out”. If a group does not use the safe harbour for a territory in one year, it cannot return to it for that territory later.

Real-calendar illustration (not the story). A group with a calendar year end can use the harbour for its year to 31 December 2026, at the 17% test: its last year. A group whose year runs 1 July 2026 – 30 June 2027 also gets that year (commencing before 31 December 2026; ending before 30 June 2028). A group with a 1 January 2027 start does not.

Worked example 30.3: the transitional safe harbour tests for Tarnmoor (invented; we run the numbers on this year’s rules)

Territory De minimis Simplified ETR (17%) Routine profits Result
Vallaria (TVS profit £30.0m in GY2; tax 20%) Fails (far above €10m / €1m) Passes (20% ≥ 17%) Not needed Top-up nil without full calculation
Marrovia (TCM, GY5) Revenue about €6.2m (< €10m) but profit about €5.9m (> €1m): fails 9% (or 13% with the CFC charge): fails Finance company with a small office: SBIE minimal: fails Full GloBE computation (worked example 30.2)

Euro figures at the invented €1.15 per £: revenue £5.4m ≈ €6.21m; profit £5.1m ≈ €5.87m.

Two other harbours to recognise. - UTPR transitional safe harbour (Sch 16 para 12A): protected the UPE’s territory where its nominal corporate rate is at least 20%, for APs commencing on or before 31 December 2025, ending before 31 December 2026, and not longer than 12 months. - QDMTT safe harbour (Sch 16A Part 1): where a group pays an accredited QDMTT in a territory, it may elect (annually, for all members there) to treat the top-up there as nil under everyone else’s rules, so one calculation does (HMRC, MTT15110–15120).

FA 2026 Sch 8 adds simplified calculations for non-material members (Sch 16A Part 3).

Registration, returns and a moving rulebook.

The administration is where an awareness question may well find its marks.

Obligation Rule Reference
Registration Filing member registers within 6 months after the end of the first AP in which the group is qualifying, even if no top-up tax is payable Sch 14 para 6
GloBE information return (GIR) 15 months after the end of the AP; 18 months for the first; no deadline before 30 June 2026 (FA 2025 Sch 4 para 52); or an overseas return notification where the GIR is filed with a qualifying authority abroad Sch 14 para 10
UK self-assessment return (MTT/DTT) Same 15/18-month timetable and 30 June 2026 floor Sch 14 para 13
Late filing (transitional) HMRC: no late filing penalties for submissions before 1 August 2026; failed-validation GIRs resubmitted by 1 September 2026 keep the original date GOV.UK “How to report Pillar 2 top-up taxes”
Payment First AP ending on or before 31 December 2024: 30 June 2026; first AP ending later: 18 months after its end; later APs: the later of 30 June 2026 and 15 months after the AP end GOV.UK “Pay Pillar 2 top-up taxes”

Tarnmoor. TPLC is the filing member. For GY5 (AP ending 31 December GY5) its GIR, its UK return and payment of the £102,000 are due by 31 March GY7 (15 months). In the group accounts the top-up is current tax, disclosed separately, with no deferred tax (IAS 12 paras 4A, 88B; chapter 6).

The rulebook keeps moving: FA 2026 s 50 and Sch 8. Changes include elective qualifying domestic top-up taxes; application of the IIR to permanent establishments; flow-through UPEs; deferred tax exclusions (APs ending on or after 21 July 2025); a qualifying undertaxed profits tax (APs beginning on or after 31 December 2025); DTT for REITs; exchange rates; group relief payments as covered taxes; CFC mobile income for DTT (cap at 15% of the CFC entity’s adjusted profits); the simplified calculations for non-material members; and a 12-month extension for pre-2026 elections. General commencement: APs beginning on or after 31 December 2025, or from 31 December 2023 by an irrevocable “retrospection election” (FA 2026 Sch 8 para 53).

Coming next: proposed, not law. In January 2026 the OECD released the “side-by-side” package, designed, as its name suggests, to let some countries’ own minimum tax systems operate alongside the GloBE rules. A ministerial statement (7 January 2026) said the UK would implement it through the Finance Bill 2026-27, and on 13 July 2026 the government published draft legislation (policy paper “Pillar 2: side-by-side package and further amendments to Multinational Top-up Tax and Domestic Top-up Tax”). The side-by-side measures would apply to APs beginning on or after 1 January 2026 and include elective safe harbours, one of which, according to professional commentary, would remove MTT for groups with US parents; further technical amendments would apply mainly from APs beginning on or after 31 December 2026. Not law, and not examinable on FA 2026.

Exam lens: Pillar Two (MTT and DTT) - Grade: Multinational Top Up Tax 3; Domestic Top Up Tax 3 (2026 grid; added at 3 for 2026; also 3 in the 2028 grid). Check the 2027 grid when published. - Past appearances: none, M23–M26. - Style: if it appears, expect a few recognition marks inside a larger group question (an acquisition taking a group over €750m; a low-tax subsidiary in a CFC question; a tax accounting tail), not a computation. - Marks likely for: the threshold (exceeds €750m in 2 of the previous 4 periods); which tax applies to which entity (IIR on the UK parent for overseas members, DTT on UK entities, UTPR as backstop); 15% and the territory-by-territory ETR; registration within 6 months; GIR and return at 15 months (18 for the first); the IAS 12 exception (no deferred tax; separate current tax). - Traps: saying every company pays 15%; attempting a full GloBE computation unasked; forgetting that a CFC charge is pushed down; stating the side-by-side package as law.

Diverted profits tax, and pay now, argue later.

Now the other half of the chapter. DPT was in FA 2015 Part 3, for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2015 (s 116; straddling periods split). It had two limbs: 1. Insufficient economic substance (ss 80–81): a UK company (or UK PE) whose arrangements with a related party involved entities or transactions lacking economic substance, producing an effective tax mismatch. 2. Avoided PE (s 86, with an exception for limited UK-related sales or expenses in s 87): a non-UK company arranging its affairs to avoid a UK taxable presence.

The rate was 25% (s 79 as enacted), set above corporation tax on purpose; for APs beginning on or after 1 April 2023 it rose to 31% (FA 2021 s 8), six points above the new 25% main rate.

The design mattered as much as the rate. HMRC issued notices, and the company had to pay before it could argue; review and appeal came later (ss 101–102). The aim was plain: a group facing an immediate cash bill at a premium rate had every reason to agree its transfer pricing on the ordinary CT basis instead.

The case: Glencore Energy UK Ltd v HMRC [2017] EWHC 1476 (Admin). HMRC issued Glencore Energy UK Ltd with a charging notice under FA 2015 s 95 for £21,129,349 plus interest, for its nine-month AP 1 April – 31 December 2015. Glencore did not wait for the statutory review and appeal; it asked the High Court for judicial review of the notice. Green J (judgment 29 June 2017) refused permission: the statute’s own route, a review under s 101 and an appeal to the First-tier Tribunal, was an adequate alternative remedy, and judicial review is a remedy of last resort; he also refused permission on wider discretionary grounds. A separate ruling held that the High Court could not grant permission to appeal its own refusal ([2017] EWHC 1587 (Admin)). Glencore appealed. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal (R (Glencore Energy UK Ltd) v HMRC [2017] EWCA Civ 1716, 2 November 2017; Gloster, Sales and Singh LJJ, Sales LJ giving the lead judgment): the statutory review and appeal were a suitable alternative remedy, and judicial review would be appropriate only in an exceptional case.

Glencore’s lesson is the one the design intended: pay now, argue later. The tax would be argued, if at all, after the money had moved.

The weakness lay elsewhere. A free-standing tax, outside corporation tax, sat awkwardly with double tax treaties and the mutual agreement procedure (MAP). That is the problem the replacement solves.

From diverted profits tax to unassessed transfer pricing profits.

FA 2026 s 46 and Sch 5 repealed FA 2015 Part 3 for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026 (Sch 5 para 1(3)). In its place is a new Part 4A of TIOPA 2010, ss 217A–217T (with Sch A1 for partnerships and Lloyd’s).

Commencement in practice (real-calendar illustration, not the Tarnmoor story):

Company’s accounting period Regime
1 January – 31 December 2026 UTPP for the whole period
1 April 2025 – 31 March 2026 DPT for the whole period; UTPP from the AP beginning 1 April 2026
1 October 2025 – 30 September 2026 DPT for the whole period, although most of it falls after 1 January 2026

Old periods keep the old tax, so an enquiry into an earlier year can still involve DPT, and an adviser must check the period before naming the charge.

Misconception: “DPT still exists.” For current periods it does not. For any AP beginning on or after 1 January 2026, the answer is UTPP, and on a paper examined on FA 2026, that is the name to use.

What UTPP taxes (s 217B). Profits that a transfer pricing requirement brings into charge but that the company has not reflected in its own return. Chapter 27 explains the TP rules themselves. The new charge has no measure of its own: it borrows the arm’s length price and taxes the gap between that price and the return. The charge is corporation tax, so (HMRC’s TIIN, 26 November 2025) treaties and MAP apply to it. The UTPP rate is the underlying CT rate plus 6% (s 217A(2)–(4)): 31% where the main rate of 25% applies (HMRC, INTM489155). DPT’s separate notification requirement has not been kept.

And the avoided-PE limb? It has no direct successor in Part 4A. On this book’s reading, that work now falls to the rewritten PE definition in FA 2026 Sch 7 (CTA 2010 s 1141(1)(b): the “principal role” test for dependent agents; chapter 23). The government has not said so in exactly those words (reasoned inference).

Three gates.

UTPP is not charged at the premium rate just because a price was wrong. Three conditions must all be met (ss 217C–217E, with s 217D on the mismatch; HMRC, INTM489105, INTM489115–489150):

Gate Test HMRC guidance
1. Effective tax mismatch outcome (ETMO) The corresponding amount (tax payable by the other party, in any period, on profits corresponding to the UTPP; may be nil) is less than 80% of the underlying CT amount (UK CT at the underlying rate on the UTPP) INTM489130–489135
2. Tax design condition (TDC) Reasonable to assume the arrangements were designed to reduce, eliminate or delay UK tax (income tax by withholding, or CT) INTM489140–489145: not the same as a “main purpose” test; UTPP does not apply merely because a group moves a whole activity to a lower-tax territory; the target is separating UK economic activity from the income it produces
3. Not excepted loan relationships The UTPP must not arise wholly from excepted loan relationship arrangements (CTA 2009 Part 5 and Part 6 deemed loan relationships, or a loan relationship with a hedging derivative under Part 7) INTM489150: a loan inside a wider arrangement does not automatically make the outcome excepted

HMRC’s own ETMO example (INTM489135): a UK company pays £20m for services with an arm’s length price of £15m. UTPP £5m; underlying CT amount £1.25m; the overseas recipient pays £1m of tax on the £5m. £1m is exactly 80% of £1.25m, so there is no ETMO. HMRC adds that the test can be revisited: if the foreign tax is later refunded (for example by loss relief), the corresponding amount falls to nil and the ETMO is met.

The third gate echoes an old trap: the M23 examiners said DPT “does not apply to loan relationships”, and UTPP keeps an equivalent exception.

Worked example 30.4: the premium (labelled hypothetical, not Tarnmoor)

For this example, suppose a UK distributor in another group overpays a royalty by £4,000,000 to a related company taxed at 5%.

£
UTPP (excess over arm’s length) 4,000,000
Underlying CT amount (25%) 1,000,000
Corresponding amount (5% × 4,000,000) 200,000
Ratio (200,000 ÷ 1,000,000) 20%: < 80%: ETMO met
If the TDC is also met: UTPP at 31% 1,240,000
CT if the company had self-assessed the adjustment (25%) 1,000,000
Premium for not self-assessing 240,000

Worked example 30.5: Tarnmoor’s provisions against the 80% gate (invented; simplified)

Counterparty territory Local rate ÷ UK 25% ETMO possible?
Vallaria 20% 80% No: 80% is not less than 80%
Marrovia 9% 36% Yes

Calder → TVS (GY3). Calder sold its process-valve customer contracts and know-how to TVS for £6.0m; the price was later raised by £2.0m in the transfer pricing settlement (chapter 27). UK CT on £2.0m at 25% = £500,000; Vallarian tax on the matching profit at 20% = £400,000 = 80%: no ETMO, so UTPP could not apply (simplification: Vallarian deductions for TVS’s own amortisation and timing are ignored). The sale also moved a real business, which on HMRC’s guidance points away from the TDC.

UK → Marrovia. A Marrovian provision would open gate 1. The only one ever proposed, Project Undertow (TFL’s £80m perpetual notes to TCM, GY4; chapter 29), was a loan relationship (gate 3 would likely have shut UTPP out anyway, and the hybrid rules were the real problem), and the board rejected it.

Pay first, and what the examiner wants.

The procedure keeps the old pay-first design, now inside corporation tax (ss 217F–217S):

Step Rule
Preliminary notice By a designated HMRC officer, no later than 4 years after the end of the AP
Representations Within 30 days (60 for transparent entities), on limited grounds
Assessment Within 60 days of the preliminary notice (90 for transparent entities), or 30 days after a closure notice if later
Period for amendments 15 months: the company may amend its return to bring the profits into ordinary CT (not in the last 21 days); HMRC may correct or increase the assessment; no closure notice before the period ends
Payment Pay first: postponement only for amounts equal to tax already paid on the corresponding profits (s 217K)
Appeal Only after paying and after the period for amendments, within 30 days; the tribunal may reduce the charge to the non-UTPP rate if a condition is not met (s 217M)
No reliefs “No relief, deduction or set-off of any description” against UTPP profits or UTPP-rate tax; no TMA s 59DA repayment claims (ss 217Q–217S)

The lesson for a tax function: the charge is a lever, not a destination. Correct transfer pricing in the company’s own return removes the exposure, and even after a notice, an amendment within the period brings the profits back to the ordinary rate.

Going further: the tax function’s tasks (Tarnmoor, invented)

Tarnmoor’s tax function, led in the story by Tom Hesketh, keeps two lists. - UTPP: every cross-border provision with a counterparty taxed at less than 80% of the UK rate (Marrovia; any new low-tax territory), with TP documentation (Master File and Local File, chapter 27) that supports the price in the return; self-assess any adjustment; brief the SAO and the audit committee on open positions. - Pillar Two: collect GloBE data from every entity well before the 15-month deadline; decide each year, territory by territory, whether a safe harbour election is available and wanted (remembering “once out, always out”); reconcile the CFC charge with the top-up so the s 179 push-down is applied once and within its cap; estimate the top-up for the accounts (separate current tax; no deferred tax) and the half-year disclosures; monitor the side-by-side legislation (proposed). - Interaction: transfer pricing (27) is the trigger for UTPP; the CFC charge (26) feeds the Marrovian ETR; deferred tax (6) excludes Pillar Two; the PE rewrite (23) replaces the avoided-PE limb.

How the examiner tests it. These topics are awareness, grade 3. None was examined M23–M26. At awareness level the marks go to recognition: a sentence or two showing the rule exists and when it applies.

DPT has a history on this paper, as a trap. After M23 Q3 (15 marks: a loan from a US company that might take 60% control; TP, CIR, withholding), the examiners reported that “time was wasted on DPT, which does not apply to loan relationships”. After N23 Q1 (20 marks: residence and a CFC finance company) they noted that some candidates “strayed into DPT and CIR”. The same discipline holds now: for any period beginning on or after 1 January 2026, say UTPP, not DPT; and do not raise it unless the question gives you a low-taxed related party, a pricing problem and a hint of design.

Exam lens: DPT and UTPP - Grade: Diverted Profits Tax 3 (2026 grid; moved from 2 in the draft 2025 grid; still 3 in the 2028 grid). The grid row says DPT; for FA 2026 periods the regime is UTPP. Check the 2027 grid’s wording. - Past appearances: never the subject of a question M23–M26; penalised as irrelevant in M23 Q3 and N23 Q1. - Style: recognition in a TP question: “the profits could be within UTPP at 31% if the 80% and design conditions are met; correct self-assessment avoids it”. - Traps: calling it DPT for current periods; raising it for loans (excepted loan relationships); forgetting it is now corporation tax (treaties and MAP apply); quoting 25% (DPT’s original rate) instead of CT rate + 6%; ignoring the commencement date (“beginning on or after 1 January 2026”).

What to take away.

Pillar Two puts a 15% floor under the profits of large multinational groups, measured territory by territory. More than 135 countries agreed it in October 2021, and the UK enacted it in F(No.2)A 2023 Parts 3–4.

Multinational top-up tax, from 31 December 2023, makes a UK parent pay top-up on low-taxed members abroad through the income inclusion rule, with the undertaxed profits rule as backstop from 31 December 2024. Domestic top-up tax collects any top-up on UK profits first.

A group is in if consolidated revenue exceeds €750m in at least two of the previous four periods (s 129). The statute says “exceeds”; some HMRC guidance says “or more”.

ETR = covered taxes ÷ GloBE income for each territory; top-up percentage = 15% − ETR, applied to profit after the substance-based income exclusion.

In our invented case, Marrovia’s 9% plus the pushed-down CFC charge of £204,000 gives 13.0% on £5.1m in GY5; TPLC pays £102,000 of MTT; everything together is exactly 15%.

The transitional CbCR safe harbour runs out with periods commencing in 2026, when its simplified ETR test is 17%; once out, always out.

Register within 6 months of the end of the first qualifying AP; file the GIR and UK return within 15 months (18 for the first). The side-by-side package is proposed, not law.

DPT ran from 1 April 2015 at 25%, later 31%, with a pay-now, argue-later design that survived the Glencore challenge. For APs beginning on or after 1 January 2026 it is repealed. UTPP is charged as corporation tax at 31% (main rate + 6%), through three gates: the other party’s tax is under 80% of the UK tax; the tax design condition is met; the profits do not arise wholly from excepted loan relationships. Pay first; no reliefs; correct pricing in the return removes the charge.

So, who collects the difference? The country where the profit arises, if it chooses to; then the parent’s country; then everyone else. And what stops profit leaving through mispricing? Transfer pricing, backed now by a premium rate of corporation tax that a group can avoid simply by getting the price right.

Next, Part Five puts it all together: chapter 31 follows a single deal, Tarnmoor’s purchase of Ridgeway from Jess Hartley, through every rule in this book.

Part Five: Putting It Together.

Chapter 31: The Ridgeway deal.

Completion day.

On 1 April, some years after the events of the last thirty chapters, Tarnmoor plc (TPLC) bought a bicycle company. The price was £4.5m in cash. The seller was Jess Hartley; the company was Ridgeway Holdings Ltd (RH), the parent of Ridgeway Cycles Ltd (RC). Our invented group, Tarnmoor, its people and its numbers are invented for teaching, as they have been throughout this book. So is Jess, whose story The Living Law (TKS) told. Ireland, which will matter later, is real, as are its 12.5% trading rate and the UK–Ireland treaty.

By Tarnmoor’s standards it was a small deal. Tarnmoor’s revenue runs to more than £1bn a year; Ridgeway’s taxable profit is about £600,000. Yet when Tom Hesketh, the group head of tax, opened the file that morning, the list of tax points ran to two pages. That is the question for this chapter: why does a small acquisition by a large group touch almost every rule in this book, and how do you find them all, in order, without missing the ones that carry marks?

This is chapter 31, the first chapter of Part Five. It is the capstone. It teaches no new rule: every rule it uses was taught earlier, and each time the owning chapter is named. What it adds is the method, the order and the interactions: what the LCG syllabus narrative calls the interaction of taxes and corporate transformations, and the way most 20-mark questions are built. It also closes the last open thread of The Living Law: the election Jess never made for her Dublin showroom.

Statutes: Corporation Tax Act 2009 (CTA 2009), Corporation Tax Act 2010 (CTA 2010), Taxation (International and Other Provisions) Act 2010 (TIOPA 2010), Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992 (TCGA 1992), and the Corporation Tax (Instalment Payments) Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/3175). As always, the numbers apply the law for FY2026 (Finance Act 2026), whatever year the story has reached.

Story time. The Ridgeway year is “some years later”: after GY7, not numbered. In this chapter RY means the Ridgeway year, and RC’s accounting periods are AP1 (1 April RY – 31 March RY+1), AP2 (1 April RY+1 – 31 March RY+2) and AP3 (1 April RY+2 – 31 March RY+3). No calendar year is attached to any of them.

The road to Ridgeway.

The Living Law followed Jess Hartley from a cycle business she ran herself, through incorporation and a holding company structure, to a group of two companies: RH owns 100% of RC, and Jess owns 100% of RH, with a base cost of £162,000. Along the way the group bought and later sold Wharfe Wheels (TKS chapter 24). RC opened a second unit in Skipton, and then a showroom in Dublin.

The Dublin showroom is a branch: a permanent establishment (PE) of RC in Ireland, not a separate company. The Living Law, chapter 26, gave its results:

Branch year Result (£) Treatment (no election)
Year 1 (80,000) Loss relieved against RC’s UK profits at once
Year 2 (30,000) Loss relieved against RC’s UK profits at once
Year 3 120,000 Taxed in the UK with credit for Irish tax
Year 4 200,000 Irish tax at 12.5%: £25,000; UK CT with credit

Jess never made the s 18A CTA 2009 election; The Living Law, chapter 26, left the question open. The Living Law, chapter 31, imagined a hypothetical £4m offer for the group “if a buyer came back tomorrow”; no sale happened. This is the real sale, at its own price: £4.5m.

RC today (invented). UK trading profit about £400,000 a year; Dublin branch profit about £200,000. RC’s year ends 31 March, so the deal falls on the first day of an AP (a change of owner never ends an AP by itself: CTA 2009 s 10). That simplifies several timing tests below.

Worked example 31.1: RC’s corporation tax before the deal (invented; £)

£
UK trading profit 400,000
Dublin branch profit (part of RC’s trading profit; no election) 200,000
TTP 600,000
CT at 25% (main rate: far above the upper limit) 150,000
Less DTR: lower of Irish tax £25,000 and UK tax on the branch profit £50,000 (TIOPA 2010 s 42) (25,000)
CT payable 125,000
Total tax, Ireland + UK 150,000

The seller’s side, in one paragraph. Jess is an individual selling shares. Her gain before costs is £4,500,000 − £162,000 = £4,338,000, charged to capital gains tax, with business asset disposal relief if she still meets its conditions (The Living Law, chapters 18 and 31). No corporation tax, no SSE, nothing for the buyer to compute. LCG does not examine it: note it in one line and move on.

Walking every floor.

An Advanced Technical question is a building inspection. A good surveyor does not wander the house looking at whatever catches the eye: she walks every floor, in the same order, with the same checklist, and records what she finds on each, including the floors where she finds nothing. The checklist is what stops her missing the damp in the cellar while admiring the roof.

Tom’s checklist for a share acquisition (the order this chapter follows):

Floor Questions Owning chapters
1. The transaction Stamp duty (and SDLT?); buyer’s costs (Centrica line); tax deed and diligence; VAT signpost 13, 20, 21
2. The target’s history Trading losses (Part 14); capital losses (Sch 7A); past intra-group transfers (degrouping); open enquiries 14, 17, 20
3. Thresholds Associated companies (two timings); QIP status (large / very large / grace); knock-on for every group company 1, 3
4. Group regimes Group relief from joining; deductions allowance nomination; shared AIA; R&D status 8, 10, 14, 15
5. Governance and compliance SAO; tax strategy; UTT; CCO; TP (SME exemption lost); CbC, master and local file; enquiry window; GPA; CIR; Pillar Two 3, 4, 27, 28, 30
6. Special features Here: the foreign branch (s 18A election; s 140; transfer to TIL; CFC) 25, 26
7. The accounts Deferred tax on fair value uplifts in the consolidation 6
8. People Retention terms; deductibility and timing (s 1288); who pays 7, 20
9. Recommendation Where asked: name the option and the main reason 25, 32

Two exam rules shape the walk. After the N25 and M26 sittings the chief examiner explained that “tax consequences” means every tax in the syllabus, including stamp duty and SDLT; a named tax means only that tax. And excluded means excluded: if the question says ignore TP, a paragraph on it earns nothing (chapter 32).

Misconception: “a small acquisition is a small tax job.” It is not. The size of the target barely matters; the size of the group it joins decides the compliance load. RC goes from a two-company family business to a member of a listed group of eleven companies that count as associated, a worldwide group for the CIR, an MNE group for Pillar Two, a group with no TP SME exemption and a group with an SAO. Almost every compliance setting changes on completion day, and some change a year later. The tax on RC’s profits hardly moves; everything around it does.

The price of the paper.

Stamp duty (chapter 21). TPLC buys shares, so the charge is stamp duty on the stock transfer form: 0.5%, rounded up to the nearest £5, payable by the buyer; the instrument must be presented for stamping within 30 days of execution, or interest and penalties run.

Worked example 31.2: stamp duty (invented)

£4,500,000 × 0.5% = £22,500 (a multiple of £5: no rounding). Payable by TPLC. Cash consideration only: no contingent element, so no “stated maximum” question (chapter 21).

  • No SDLT: RC’s Skipton property stays inside RC; only shares change hands.
  • No stamp duty group relief (FA 1930 s 42): the transferor is an individual, and relief needs a 75% relationship between transferor and transferee.
  • Base cost: the £22,500 is an incidental cost of acquisition (TCGA 1992 s 38), not deductible for CT. TPLC’s base cost in RH is £4,522,500. It will rarely matter: after 12 months a later sale should be within the SSE (TCGA 1992 Sch 7AC; chapter 18).

TPLC’s other costs follow the line chapter 13 drew for Calder after Centrica Overseas Holdings Ltd v HMRC [2024] UKSC 25: costs of appraising whether to invest at all can be management expenses; once the board decides to acquire this target, the costs of acquiring it are capital (CTA 2009 s 1219(3)(a)). HMRC’s view (CTM08190, CTM08260) puts the boundary, at the earliest, at the decision to acquire a particular target. Tom asks for the date of the board decision, because the invoices fall either side of it.

The contract (chapter 20). A buyer of shares inherits the company’s past, so tax that belongs to Jess’s years must stay Jess’s. Tarnmoor’s diligence looks hardest at: 1. Branch attribution: the profit RC has attributed to Dublin; Irish and UK figures must agree. 2. Payroll: employment taxes are where owner-managed companies most often slip. 3. Returns and enquiries: nothing open with HMRC.

The tax deed makes Jess liable for tax arising from pre-completion periods, with payments treated as a reduction in the price.

VAT (outside LCG): RC might join Tarnmoor’s VAT group; a decision for another adviser.

Exam lens: the transaction - Grades: stamp duty on stocks and shares 3 (awareness); companies with investment business (deal costs) 1. - Past appearances: N24 Q5 gave 3 of its 20 marks to stamp duty on a share purchase (0.5%, 30 days, buyer pays); M23 Q6 (10 marks) was entirely acquisition costs. - Traps: deducting stamp duty; charging SDLT on a share purchase; giving stamp duty group relief on a purchase from an individual; missing stamp duty altogether when “tax consequences” are asked (chapter 32).

Counting the family again.

The third floor is where most candidates lose marks. Associated companies (chapter 3; CTA 2010 s 18E): one controls the other, or both are under common control; overseas companies count; a company carrying on no trade or business is ignored.

Is RH a passive holding company? (CTA 2010 s 18F.) RH controls RC, so it would count. But s 18F treats certain holding companies as carrying on no business, so they are ignored under s 18E(3). The company must:

Condition (s 18F) RH (invented facts)
Carry on a business of making investments, and no trade Yes: it only holds the RC shares
Have one or more 51% subsidiaries Yes: RC (100%)
Be passive throughout the AP: no assets other than shares in its 51% subsidiaries Yes, provided it holds no cash and makes no loans
…and no income other than dividends which it redistributes to its shareholders (the redistribution condition) Yes, provided any dividend from RC is paid straight up to TPLC in the same period

In our invented case RH meets the conditions. The integration plan therefore says: RH keeps no bank balance, lends nothing, and passes on any dividend in the same period. Break any of those and RH starts to count.

Tarnmoor’s companies that count (after the Tarnwater demerger, the sale of TAL and the strike-off of dormant Tarnmoor Pumps): TPLC, TEL, CVE, TES, TFL, BSL, HEL, TVS, TCM, TIL = 10. RC makes 11.

The two timings (chapter 3):

Purpose When associates count Authority
Small profits rate and marginal relief Associated at any time in the AP CTA 2010 s 18E; CTM03580
QIP thresholds (£1.5m large, £20m very large, £10m grace limit) As at the day before the AP begins HMRC’s reading of SI 1998/3175 reg 3: CTM92530, COM95001

Worked example 31.3: RC’s instalment status, AP1 to AP3 (invented; HMRC’s counting dates)

AP1 AP2 AP3
Associates for marginal relief (divisor) 10 (11): limits £4,545 / £22,727 10 (11) 10 (11)
QIP counting date 31 March RY (owned via RH, passive; Jess owns no other company that counts) 31 March RY+1 31 March RY+2
QIP divisor 1 11 11
Large threshold (£) 1,500,000 136,364 136,364
Very large threshold (£) 20,000,000 1,818,182 1,818,182
Grace limit £10m ÷ divisor (£) 10,000,000 909,091 909,091
Augmented profits (forecast) (£) 600,000 400,000 (after the election) 400,000
Large? No Yes, but grace: not large in the previous 12 months and profits ≤ £909,091 (reg 3(5)) Yes: large in AP2, and the grace year counts as a year of being large
Payment 9 months and 1 day after the AP: 1 January RY+2 1 January RY+3 QIPs: 3/12 × CT ≈ £100,000 = 4 × £25,000 in months 7, 10, 13, 16 (14 October RY+2; 14 January, 14 April, 14 July RY+3)

The marginal relief divisor changes nothing in practice: RC’s profits were already far above the upper limit, so it already paid at 25%. (Checked in Python: 1,500,000/11 = 136,363.6; 20,000,000/11 = 1,818,181.8; 10,000,000/11 = 909,090.9.)

Status of the AP3 conclusion. CTM92530 states the grace test (profits ≤ £10m, divided, and not large in the previous 12 months, reg 3(5)); HMRC’s manual and practitioners’ worked examples treat the grace year as a year in which the company was large, so the grace is available only once. The regulation’s current text was not opened for this book: cite reg 3(5) and HMRC’s reading.

The ripple through the group. For their AP containing 1 April RY, Tarnmoor’s 31 December companies have 11 associates for marginal relief (RC is associated for part of the AP). For QIPs their count changes only from the AP beginning the following 1 January: divisor 11, large £136,364, very large £1,818,182. A £600,000 business has moved every instalment threshold in the group.

Exam lens: thresholds - Grades: calculation of liability 1; administration and payment of tax 1. - Past appearances: N24 Q5 gave 4 marks to filing and instalments for a newly acquired company. - Traps: one timing for both purposes; counting a passive holding company or a dormant company; forgetting that overseas companies count; giving a very large company a year of grace (there is none: CTM92520, CTM92800); forgetting that the £10m grace limit is divided too. - Layout: a short table per AP: counting date, divisor, thresholds, status, payment dates.

What the shares bring with them.

The target’s history (floor 2) is short here, and a nil answer with a reason still scores.

  • Trading losses: none. The Dublin losses were relieved long ago against RC’s own profits. CTA 2010 Part 14 (chapter 14’s Brackenwell analysis) has nothing to restrict.
  • Capital losses: none, so the pre-entry loss rules (TCGA 1992 Sch 7A; chapter 17) are silent.
  • Degrouping: if RH and RC had moved an asset between them at no gain, no loss within the last six years, s 179 would be the worry. It is not: they leave Jess’s ownership together, RC remaining RH’s subsidiary throughout (the “associated companies leaving together” exception, s 179(2), Condition B), and RH’s group becomes part of Tarnmoor’s (s 170(10)). Chapter 17.

Group regimes switch on (floor 4).

Regime What happens Authority (chapter)
Group relief RC and RH join TPLC’s group relief group on completion (1 April RY); no relief before then. RC’s AP (to 31 March) and the 31 December companies’ APs overlap only partly: relief is limited by the overlapping period on each side. The same arrangements analysis as chapter 15 applies to the heads of terms with Jess: group relief with Tarnmoor companies starts only on completion CTA 2010 ss 139–142, 154 (15)
Deductions allowance RH and RC countersign TPLC’s standing nomination; RC has no losses, so nothing turns on it now, but a company left out gets no allowance CTA 2010 ss 269ZR ff (14)
AIA One £1m for all members’ chargeable periods ending in the same financial year to 31 March (parent test at the end of each period). RC’s AP1 ends 31 March RY+1: it shares the allowance with the 31 December RY periods of Tarnmoor’s companies, which ended nine months earlier. RC gets whatever the group allocates CAA 2001 s 51C; Interpretation Act 1978 (8)
R&D RC is now linked to a large enterprise: not an SME for any purpose. Any claim is under the merged scheme’s expenditure credit (20%, taxable, set against the liability); ERIS is out of reach; HMRC’s view is that a company taken over is large for the whole AP of the takeover (here the AP begins on completion anyway) CTA 2009 Part 13; CIRD92000 (10)

Exam lens: target history and group regimes - Grades: use of losses 1; groups and companies leaving groups 1; group relief 1; R&D 1; capital allowances 1. - Traps: restricting losses that do not exist; missing the overlapping-period limit on group relief for non-coterminous APs; treating RC as still an SME for R&D.

The compliance settings change.

Floor 5 is the one candidates under-sell. N24 Q5 (20 marks) set exactly this scenario: a US multinational bought a UK SME, and candidates had to explain its new obligations. The marking guide gave 6.5 marks to transfer pricing alone.

Setting RC and RH after completion Authority (chapter)
Transfer pricing In Jess’s hands RC was a small enterprise: TP did not apply (TIOPA 2010 s 166). Size is measured across linked enterprises; linked to Tarnmoor, RC is large: TP applies from completion. Dealings with UK group companies are within the UK-to-UK exemption (s 164A; chargeable periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026), but s 164A does not apply to activities in relation to which s 18A exemption adjustments are made (below) TIOPA 2010 ss 164A, 166, 172 (27)
CbC, master file, local file RC enters TPLC’s CbC report and master file; the Dublin PE’s figures appear under Ireland; local file for material cross-border dealings SI 2016/237; SI 2023/818 (27)
SAO Turns on UK incorporation (both are English). A company qualifies for a financial year only if it was a group member at the end of its preceding financial year. RC’s previous FY ended 31 March RY, the day before completion: first SAO year = AP2 (1 April RY+1 – 31 March RY+2); Nadia Kerr’s certificate due 9 months after that FY (31 December RY+2). Same for RH FA 2009 Sch 46; SAOG11260 (4)
Tax strategy Covered by TPLC’s published group strategy (published by 31 December each year) FA 2016 Sch 19 (4)
UTT RC and RH are members of a 51% group above the £200m UK turnover test: notify uncertain treatments over the £5m threshold in their returns (unlikely at this size, but the question must be asked) FA 2022 Sch 17 (4)
CCO Tarnmoor’s reasonable prevention procedures must now reach the Dublin showroom, whose staff are associated persons of RC; the foreign tax evasion facilitation offence (s 46) is the relevant one Criminal Finances Act 2017 ss 45–46 (4)
Enquiry window Member of a group that is not small: 12 months from the filing date FA 1998 Sch 18 para 24 (3)
GPA Requires the same accounting date: RC (31 March) cannot join Tarnmoor’s group payment arrangement until it moves to 31 December (Calder joined only after its move, GY4) TMA 1970 s 59F (3)
CIR RC and RH join the worldwide group. Under the FA 2026 rules (periods of account ending on or after 31 March 2026) TPLC must be appointed reporting company for each period by more than half of the eligible UK companies: RC and RH are now two of them. Tarnmoor still carries disallowed interest forward from earlier years, so interest capacity has value; RC’s taxable profits add to aggregate tax-EBITDA TIOPA 2010 Part 10; Sch 7A para 1 (FA 2026 s 61) (28)
Pillar Two Revenue far above €750m: RH and RC are constituent entities at once; DTT covers UK entities; the Dublin PE is treated as a separate constituent entity located in Ireland F(No.2)A 2023 Parts 3–4 (30)

Exam lens: joining a large group - Grades: SAO 1; tax strategy 1; CCO 1; UTT 3; TP 1; CIR 1; MTT/DTT 3. - N24 Q5 (20 marks) marking guide (as recorded in chapter 20): filing and instalments 4, CbC 3, TP 6.5 (SME exemption lost; master and local file), CIR 3.5 (probably no restriction, but file to protect the position; reporting company; abbreviated return), stamp duty 3. The examiners reported that most candidates found TP, but some wrote at length on it and ignored easier points, and some raised hybrids with nothing in the question to trigger them. - Traps: the SAO year of joining (the test looks at the end of the preceding FY); assuming UK-to-UK TP applies (s 164A) or, conversely, forgetting its carve-outs; applying the SAO to a company because it is UK resident rather than UK incorporated.

The Dublin question.

Floor 6 is the one Jess left unfinished. Chapter 25 owns the rules; three options are on the table:

  1. Elect under CTA 2009 s 18A;
  2. Incorporate the branch into a new Irish subsidiary of RC (TCGA 1992 s 140);
  3. Transfer the branch to Tarnmoor Ireland Ltd (TIL).

The election (s 18A). Once it takes effect, exemption adjustments remove the profits and losses of every foreign PE of the company. The branch’s profit is measured as the UK–Ireland treaty’s business profits article would attribute it (Ireland is a full treaty territory: s 18R). Irish tax on exempt profits is not creditable (TIOPA 2010 s 18(3A)).

Feature Rule Authority
Scope All foreign PEs of the company, present and future, in every country s 18A
Start The relevant day: the start of the company’s next AP after the election is made s 18F(1)–(2); INTM281020
Revocation Possible only before the relevant day; afterwards irrevocable (ends only if the company ceases to be UK resident) s 18F(6)–(8)
Guard rail Profits that would pass the CFC gateway are not exempt unless a CFC entity exemption (as adapted) applies ss 18G–18I
Transition Opening negative amount: 6-year look-back ss 18J–18N; INTM284020–284040

The opening negative amount. A company cannot take UK relief for branch losses and then elect just as the branch turns profitable. HMRC’s guidance (INTM284020): look back over the 6 years before the first AP the election covers; net PE losses not matched by subsequent profits in that period form the total opening negative amount, however the losses were relieved (sideways, carried back or group relief). Until it is matched by later PE profits, those profits are not exempt (INTM284030).

Worked example 31.4: RC’s look-back (invented; £)

Branch year Result Cumulative
Year 1 (80,000) (80,000)
Year 2 (30,000) (110,000)
Year 3 120,000 10,000
Year 4 200,000 210,000
Later years (about £200,000 a year) profits rising

The £110,000 of losses was matched within the next year, with £10,000 to spare, and every year since has been profitable. Whatever the 6-year window ending 31 March RY+1 catches, the net result inside it is a profit: no opening negative amount. (If the window no longer reaches Years 1–2, it contains only profits; if it does, the later profits match them.) No streaming election is needed: there is only one territory.

Worked example 31.5: RC with and without the election, a full year from AP2 (invented; £)

No election Election
UK trading profit 400,000 400,000
Dublin branch profit 200,000 exempt (s 18A)
TTP 600,000 400,000
CT at 25% 150,000 100,000
DTR (Irish tax; s 42 limit £50,000) (25,000) none: s 18(3A)
UK CT 125,000 100,000
Irish tax at 12.5% 25,000 25,000
Total tax 150,000 125,000
Saving before interactions 25,000

Test the £25,000 against the rest of the building. A capstone answer checks each interaction:

  1. CIR (chapter 28). Tax-EBITDA is built from the company’s taxable profits, so once the branch is exempt its £200,000 leaves RC’s taxable profits and the group’s aggregate tax-EBITDA (this book’s reading of TIOPA 2010 s 406: exempt PE profits never enter TTP). At 30% that is £60,000 of interest capacity. If the group is restricted, or is still reactivating disallowed interest brought forward, that capacity is worth up to £15,000 of tax (£60,000 × 25%); if the group has capacity to spare, nothing.
  2. Pillar Two (chapter 30). Without the election, the UK CT on the branch profit is allocated to the PE under the GloBE rules’ allocation of covered taxes (OECD Model Rules Art 4.3.2, as implemented; secondary sources), so the PE bears tax at the UK rate. With the election, it bears only Ireland’s 12.5%, below 15%. On a simplified view (no substance-based income exclusion; the PE blended with TIL in the Irish computation at the same rate): (15% − 12.5%) × £200,000 = up to £5,000 a year of top-up. Who collects it depends on Irish law, which this book does not teach; either way it is a group cost.
  3. TP (chapter 27). s 164A does not apply to activities for which s 18A exemption adjustments are made: if TPLC charges RC for services used in Dublin, that charge must be at arm’s length.
  4. The guard rail (ss 18G–18I). A retail showroom is far from the anti-diversion rule; its profits are also within the low profits exemption (£500,000, non-trading income ≤ £50,000) that s 18I borrows from the CFC code.
  5. Attribution (chapters 23–24). Without the election, the split between Skipton and Dublin only moved the credit around; with it, every pound attributed to Dublin is taxed at 12.5%, not 25%. HMRC will test the split: document it on arm’s length principles.
Election: net annual effect (£) Best case Worst case
UK CT saved 25,000 25,000
Lost interest capacity (60,000 × 25%) — (15,000)
Pillar Two top-up (simplified) — (5,000)
Net saving 25,000 5,000

The election never costs money on these facts while the branch is profitable; its real price is the loss of UK relief for any future branch loss of RC, anywhere.

Two other doors.

Option 2: incorporate under TCGA 1992 s 140 (chapter 25).

s 140 condition RC → new Irish subsidiary
UK resident company carrying on a trade outside the UK through a PE Yes
Transfers the trade with all its assets, or all except cash Can be arranged
To a non-UK resident company Only if the new company is genuinely managed and controlled in Ireland (chapter 22): decisions taken in Leeds would make it UK resident and the relief would fail
Consideration wholly or partly securities Shares issued to RC
Transferor holds ≥ 25% of the ordinary share capital 100%
Result Net gain postponed × securities ÷ total consideration; crystallises if RC disposes of the shares, or the subsidiary disposes of the assets within 6 years

Postponement is all it gives. The branch’s goodwill and customer relationships are intangible fixed assets, dealt with under CTA 2009 Part 8 (chapter 11), not the gains rules; its plant leaves RC’s pools with balancing adjustments (chapter 8).

Worked example 31.6: the new subsidiary through the CFC order of attack (labelled alternative, not story)

Step Analysis Result
CFC? Non-UK resident company controlled by UK persons (RC, TPLC) Yes
Exempt period Not relevant (a new company, not a newly acquired one) —
Excluded territories (Ch 11) Ireland’s place on the SI 2012/3024 list was not confirmed for this book (secondary sources report Ireland was removed from the pre-2013 list in 2002): do not rely on it Not relied on
Low profits (Ch 12) Profits about £200,000 ≤ £500,000; non-trading income ≤ £50,000 Exempt: stop
(For completeness) Low profit margin (Ch 13) A retailer’s margin over relevant operating expenditure is likely above 10% Not needed
(For completeness) Tax exemption (Ch 14) Irish tax 12.5% < 75% × 25% = 18.75% Fails
If the showroom grew beyond the low profits limit Trading profits gateway (Ch 4): where are the significant people functions? The safe harbour’s export-of-UK-goods condition needs a careful look, since the showroom sells bicycles made in Skipton Analyse then

TIOPA 2010 Part 9A: ss 371LB (low profits), 371NB (tax exemption); chapter 26.

So the subsidiary reaches the same 12.5% as the elected branch by a longer road: a transfer, a new company, residence management, TP on every bicycle Skipton sells to Dublin (RC is no longer an SME), an annual CFC review, and Irish rules on dividends paid to a UK parent (not taught here). Its one advantage is that RC stays free of an irrevocable election.

Option 3: transfer the branch to TIL.

  • s 140 fails: if RC took new TIL shares, it would hold a tiny fraction of a much larger company, far below 25%; cash consideration fails the securities condition anyway.
  • No s 171 no gain, no loss: TIL has been non-UK resident since 30 June GY4 (chapter 22); the Dublin assets would not be chargeable assets in its hands (s 171(1A)).
  • Intangibles: a cross-border related-party transfer is at an arm’s length value (FA 2026 Sch 6; chapter 11), so realisation credits arise now.
  • Commercially, it moves a bicycle showroom into a valve distributor. Reject.

EU-derived relief. Ireland, unlike the invented Vallaria of chapter 25, is a member State, so TCGA 1992 s 140C (transfer of a PE business in a member State to a company resident in a member State) is at least in view. Chapter 25 explained that its post-Brexit wording was not confirmed (non-core, grade 2). Tom does not rely on it.

Worked example 31.7: the three options side by side (invented)

(1) Elect (2) Irish subsidiary (s 140) (3) Transfer to TIL
Rate on Dublin profits 12.5% (Irish only) 12.5% (Irish only) 12.5%
One-off UK tax None Gains postponed; IFA credits and CA balancing adjustments Gains and IFA credits now
Annual saving v today £25,000 (less interactions: £5,000–£25,000 net) Similar, less running costs Similar, after an up-front charge
Future branch losses of RC No UK relief, anywhere RC unaffected; subsidiary’s losses stay in Ireland —
Extra compliance Attribution file New company; CMC; TP; CFC review TP; CFC position of TIL
Reversible? No (after the relevant day) Sell or liquidate —
Verdict Recommended Viable, longer road Rejected

Exam lens: the branch - Grade: core (1): “Company residence and chargeable profits of non-UK resident companies and concept of permanent establishment/branch”; CFCs 1; ss 140A–140L non-core (2). - Past appearances: M23 Q2 (15: stay non-exempt, elect or incorporate; recommend; “Some failed to give the recommendation and lost marks”); N25 Q2 (15: PE, credit relief, the election, incorporation; few saw that the incorporation gain could be postponed); M26 Q5 (20: PE, branch taxation and DTR, the election and its timing, subsidiary, CMC, CFC, dividend exemption; TP excluded). - Traps: treating the election as per branch; forgetting it starts from the next AP; ignoring the opening negative amount (or computing one where later profits have matched the losses); giving credit for Irish tax on exempt profits; forgetting the 25% condition in s 140; discussing the UK company’s own residence in a PE question (M26 Q5). - Layout: options in turn; a short table of UK tax with and without the election, all in £; the look-back table; recommendation naming the option and the main reason.

The recommendation.

Tom’s paper to the boards of TPLC and RC, in our invented case, recommends the election, for three reasons:

  1. It removes the UK top-up on the Dublin profit: up to £25,000 a year, and at least £5,000 after the CIR and Pillar Two interactions.
  2. Its cost fits the facts: RC has no other foreign branches and no plans for any; if Tarnmoor ever wants a loss-making venture abroad it can put it in another company (the election belongs to a company, not a group).
  3. Unlike incorporation it needs no transfer, no new company and no annual CFC review.

Timing. RC makes the election during AP1; the relevant day is 1 April RY+1, the start of AP2. AP1’s Dublin profit is still taxed in the UK with credit (UK CT £125,000 for AP1); the exemption runs from AP2 (UK CT £100,000 a year). While the heads of terms were being drafted, Tom noticed that an election made by Jess’s RC before completion would have had a relevant day of 1 April RY and exempted AP1 as well. He chose not to ask for it: it would have been an irrevocable choice made before Tarnmoor’s due diligence had finished, for a prize of £25,000. In our invented case the board minute records that reasoning; the election is made after board approval, and the minute and a copy of the election go on the permanent file.

Coming next (proposed, not law). Draft legislation for the Finance Bill 2026-27 (13 July 2026) would make the foreign branch exemption compulsory for APs beginning on or after 1 January 2027 and replace the opening negative amount rules (ss 18J–18O would be omitted, per the draft) with restrictions on carrying forward PE losses (chapter 25). Under FA 2026, which the 2027 sittings test, it is still an election. RC has no branch losses to carry forward, so its answer would not change if the draft became law. Check the Autumn Budget (28 October 2026) and the Bill as introduced.

Year end. If Tarnmoor later moves RC to 31 December, as it did with Calder, re-run the election timing and the instalment tests, because both key off the dates of APs (HMRC: a change of accounting date after the election does not move the relevant day; chapter 25).

Going further: integrating Ridgeway (the tax function’s diary) - Day 1: present the stock transfer form and pay stamp duty within 30 days (£22,500); RH and RC countersign the deductions allowance nomination; add both to the CIR authorisation list, the master file and CbC data, and the Pillar Two data set; brief RH’s directors on the s 18F conditions. - During AP1: board approval and election under s 18A (relevant day 1 April RY+1); attribution study for Dublin; CCO risk assessment for the Irish showroom; agree RC’s AIA allocation for the year to 31 March RY+1. - Treasury: no QIPs for AP1 or AP2; first QIP 14 October RY+2 (AP3, month 7). - SAO: RC and RH within Nadia Kerr’s certificate from AP2 (due 31 December RY+2). - Group accounts: purchase price allocation and deferred tax finalised within the IFRS 3 measurement period. - People: diary the retention bonus payment (1 April RY+2) and the s 1288 consequences. - Ethics: using an election Parliament offers, for the purpose for which it was offered, is ordinary tax management, not avoidance; documenting the reasons protects the next finance director.

The group accounts.

Floor 7 is not tax law, and it is where the examiner’s tax accounting marks hide. Under IFRS 3, Tarnmoor’s consolidated accounts record RC’s identifiable assets at acquisition-date fair value. The valuers identify a brand and customer relationships, never recognised in RC’s own accounts, worth £0.8m between them.

A share purchase changes nothing in RC’s tax position: RC built the brand itself (no tax cost), and TPLC’s purchase of shares gives no step-up. So in the group accounts the assets’ carrying amount exceeds their tax base by £0.8m: a taxable temporary difference (IAS 12 para 19). Chapter 6 owns the rules.

Worked example 31.8: deferred tax on the fair value uplift (invented; £)

£
Fair value of brand and customer relationships (group accounts) 800,000
Tax base (internally generated; share purchase gives no step-up) nil
Taxable temporary difference 800,000
Deferred tax liability at 25% 200,000
Entry Dr Goodwill 200,000; Cr Deferred tax liability 200,000 (IAS 12 para 66)
Deferred tax on goodwill itself None (para 15(a)): goodwill is a residual

As the group accounts amortise the customer relationships, the DTL unwinds through the deferred tax credit, so the non-deductible amortisation does not distort the group ETR. If the brand is given an indefinite life and not amortised, its part of the DTL remains. RC’s own (FRS 101) accounts and tax return are unaffected.

Two further points. IFRS 3 allows a measurement period (up to one year from acquisition) to finalise the fair values, so the DTL and goodwill can move during it. And any Pillar Two top-up the Dublin PE might bear creates no deferred tax: the IAS 12 exception (para 4A) applies (chapter 6).

Planning: document the purchase price allocation. The split between net assets, identified intangibles and goodwill drives the deferred tax, impairment testing and, later, the gain on any sale. Tom files the valuers’ report with the acquisition papers, alongside the board minute on the election.

Exam lens: deferred tax on an acquisition - Grade: deferred tax 1. - What scores: the temporary difference and why it arises (no tax step-up on a share deal); the rate and the figure; where the debit goes (goodwill); no DTL on goodwill. - Traps: recognising the DTL in the subsidiary’s own accounts; charging it to profit or loss at acquisition; using 19% because the subsidiary is small (the rate is the one expected to apply: 25% for RC).

Keeping Jess.

Floor 8 is people. Tarnmoor wants Jess to stay, so in our invented case she remains managing director of RC for two years, on a salary of £90,000 a year, with a retention bonus of £60,000 payable 24 months after completion if she is still employed. RC pays both, because it is RC’s trade she serves. Chapter 20 explained why that matters: if TPLC paid, it would be paying for services to another company and might get no deduction.

The salary is an ordinary trading deduction. The bonus is a timing puzzle under CTA 2009 s 1288 (chapter 7): remuneration charged in the accounts but not paid within 9 months after the end of the period of account is deductible only in the period in which it is paid.

Worked example 31.9: when the retention bonus is deductible (invented; £)

Assumption: RC accrues the bonus evenly over the service period, £30,000 in each of AP1 and AP2. Payment date: 1 April RY+2, the first day of AP3.

AP1 (to 31 Mar RY+1) AP2 (to 31 Mar RY+2) AP3 (to 31 Mar RY+3)
Accounts charge 30,000 30,000 —
Paid within 9 months of the period end? No: paid 12 months after (deadline 31 Dec RY+1) Yes: paid 1 day after (deadline 31 Dec RY+2) —
Tax deduction nil 30,000 30,000 (AP1’s accrual, when paid)
Tax value at 25% — 7,500 7,500

Total deduction £60,000 either way; s 1288 only moves £30,000 of it into AP3. In a computation prepared within the 9 months, assume unpaid and amend later if it is paid in time (s 1289(3)). The AP1 add-back is a short-term timing difference: a deferred tax asset of £7,500 in RC’s AP1 accounts.

An adviser’s check. The bonus must genuinely be pay for continued service: conditional on employment, at a commercial level. If the facts showed it was really part of the price for Jess’s shares, RC would be paying a capital sum on its shareholder’s behalf and would get no deduction (CTA 2009 s 54: wholly and exclusively). The service condition and the market level of the pay are the evidence. The same applies to any compensation if Jess left early: HMRC’s view (BIM38380–BIM38390; chapter 20) is that a payment connected with a change of ownership is unlikely to be wholly and exclusively for the trade.

Dan. One line for the other Hartley in these pages: Dan Hartley, made redundant when Calder closed his division on 30 September GY3, is working elsewhere now. This book leaves his later career where it found it: open.

Exam lens: people on an acquisition - Grade: CT relief for expenses relating to employment including remuneration 1; general calculation rules (Part 20 CTA 2009) 1. - Past appearances: M23 Q6 (10 marks: due diligence, legal fees, a loan arrangement fee, compensation for loss of office, retention bonuses; candidates generally did well); s 1288 in N25 (bonuses paid after the period end). - Traps: deducting an accrued bonus in the period of accrual when it is paid more than 9 months later; letting the parent pay for a subsidiary’s employee; ignoring the purpose question for change-of-control payments.

How the examiner would mark it.

Set this deal as a 20-mark question: about 42 minutes at roughly 2.1 minutes a mark. Marking guides give 0.5–1 mark per point, so a 20-mark answer needs roughly 20–40 distinct, findable points (chapter 32).

Order of work. 1. Bank the quick marks (one line each, with a reason): stamp duty £22,500, buyer, 30 days; the associated company count and the two timings; no QIPs in AP1 (divisor 1), grace in AP2 (divisor 11; £909,091), QIPs from AP3; SAO from AP2; TP switched on (SME exemption lost); CIR and Pillar Two membership. 2. Score the nils: no losses to restrict; no degrouping charge; no SDLT. A correct nil with its reason is a point like any other. 3. The branch, where the recommendation marks live: the three options in turn; the tax table with and without the election (all in £); the opening negative amount test and its result; the s 140 conditions and why the TIL route fails; the CFC position of a subsidiary; then recommend, naming the option and the main reason. 4. Accounts and people if the requirement reaches them: the DTL and its debit; the s 1288 timing.

Two disciplines. Do not restate Jess’s history: the marker knows it. And if the question names corporation tax only, Jess’s CGT and the stamp duty are outside it, however much you know about them.

Exam lens: the multi-issue question - Grade: application across the grid; the LCG narrative’s “interaction of taxes” and “corporate transformations”. - Style: technical prose and short computations; no letter or report format; “Explain”, “Calculate, with explanations”, “Recommend”. - Favourite combinations it mirrors: sale or purchase of a subsidiary + SSE + change of ownership + enquiries (M24 Q3); PE + branch exemption + incorporation + CFC (M23 Q2, N25 Q2, M26 Q5); a newly acquired company’s obligations (N24 Q5). - Traps: padding (M26 Q1 examiners: adequate but padded); hybrids or DPT with no trigger (N24 Q5; chapter 30: DPT is repealed for APs beginning on or after 1 January 2026); missing the recommendation (M23 Q2); mixing £ and £000 in one table.

What to take away.

  • A small acquisition is not a small tax job: the size of the group the target joins sets the compliance load.
  • Walk every floor in order: transaction, history, thresholds, group regimes, governance and compliance, special features, accounts, people, recommendation.
  • Stamp duty £4.5m × 0.5% = £22,500, paid by TPLC within 30 days; part of the cost of the shares; no SDLT; no group relief from an individual.
  • RH is a passive holding company (CTA 2010 s 18F): no assets but subsidiary shares, no income but redistributed dividends. Keep it passive.
  • RC’s associates: 10 (divisor 11) for marginal relief at once; for QIPs counted the day before each AP: divisor 1 in AP1 (not large), 11 in AP2 (large at £136,364, but grace: profits ≤ £909,091 and not large before), QIPs from AP3 (about 4 × £25,000).
  • Nothing to restrict: no losses, no capital losses, no degrouping charge.
  • Switched on at completion: group relief (overlapping periods), the deductions allowance nomination, a share of the single AIA, RDEC only; TP (SME exemption lost; s 164A for UK-to-UK dealings); CbC and master file; UTT; CCO procedures reaching Dublin; CIR worldwide group and reporting company authorisation; Pillar Two. SAO from AP2.
  • Dublin: elect under s 18A during AP1, effective from 1 April RY+1; no opening negative amount (losses £110,000 matched by Years 3–4 profits £320,000); UK CT £125,000 → £100,000, saving up to £25,000 a year, perhaps as little as £5,000 after lost interest capacity (up to £15,000) and simplified Pillar Two top-up (up to £5,000). Irrevocable after the relevant day; covers all future PEs of RC. s 140 incorporation only postpones gains and creates a CFC (low profits exemption today); transfer to TIL fails the 25% test and s 171. The compulsory exemption in the draft Finance Bill 2026-27 is proposed, not law.
  • Group accounts: fair value uplift £0.8m → DTL £200,000, debited to goodwill; none on goodwill.
  • Jess: MD for two years at £90,000; retention bonus £60,000 paid by RC on 1 April RY+2: £30,000 deductible in AP2, £30,000 in AP3 (s 1288).

So why does a small deal touch every rule in the book? Because a company joining a group inherits the group’s thresholds, regimes and obligations, some at once and some one period later. The answer to Jess’s last open question is yes, elect: under the law the 2027 sittings test it is still a choice, and on these facts it is a good one.

One chapter remains. Chapter 32 turns from the law to the craft: how to put all of this in front of a marker, in three and a half hours, in a form the marker can reward.

Chapter thirty-two: The Advanced Technical craft.

One sentence in the instructions.

In the Candidate Instructions for the October 2026 sitting, the Chartered Institute of Taxation (CIOT) printed a sentence every candidate should learn by heart: “Calculations left in the spreadsheet and not copied to the answer box will not be marked.”

That sentence arrived with new exam software. From October 2026 the CIOT’s papers are sat on RM Assessment Master, which replaced Exam4 (every question paper from May 2023 to May 2026 still told candidates to type their answers “as indicated by the Exam4 guidance”). The new system puts a spreadsheet on the screen, right under the place where you type your answer. It is a gift and a trap: you can add up a capital allowances pool in seconds, and if you leave it there the marker never sees it.

The sentence is a fair summary of the whole paper. The Advanced Technical paper does not reward what you know. It rewards what you put in front of the marker, in a form the marker can credit, within three and a half hours.

This chapter is about that craft. It is not question practice: you have the CIOT’s past papers and your own question bank for that. It is the set of habits that turns thirty-one chapters of law into marks. The chapter gathers what every Exam lens box in this book has said, adds the facts about the paper and the day, and checks them against the CIOT’s own documents. The law for a 2027 sitting is almost certainly FY2026 law under FA 2026, which is the law this book teaches.

Chapter 2 began this work with “Research in the exam room”. Here we finish it. There is no syllabus grade for this chapter, because its subject is the paper as a whole. Every grade quoted comes from the 2026 syllabus grid, and every comment about past papers comes from the question papers, suggested answers and examiners’ reports the CIOT publishes for each sitting (sittings are abbreviated M23 = May 2023, N23 = November 2023, and so on). Where a figure is the book’s own arithmetic rather than the CIOT’s statement, it is labelled “derived”.

The question for the chapter: what does this paper reward, and how do you give it that in 210 minutes?

The shape of the paper.

Feature Detail Status
